The Tārārahasya,
composed by the venerable Brahmānanda Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka.
The Tārārahasya.
First Chapter.
Oṃ, homage to Tārā!
To Tārā, the essence of cyclic existence, the mother of the three worlds, the bestower of all accomplishments.
Having prostrated before her who is the primordial of all, who possesses every form, who consists of all virtues, who is saluted by hosts of gods,
who bestows fearlessness from the fear of worldly existence, and who shines resplendently upon the divine royal lotus— I, named Brahmānanda, shall expound that secret for the welfare of the world.

Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Umāpati, having meditated upon this Mother of the World— who bestows liberation and is the river of nectar— carry out the creation, preservation, and dissolution of the three worlds; if a person, with their mind fixed on Her through devotion, should worship Tārā with diligence.
He who abandons this very state which brings security falls downward.

If a person, having understood the secret of Tārā, worships the king of mantras that grants liberation (tāraka), they shall obtain the most excellent accomplishment, which is difficult even for the best of gods and men to attain through other means than Tārā. Abandoning Tārā, one certainly falls into the well of delusion, the abode of extreme misfortunes.
Suffering and sorrow, as well as even a correct course of action, will never at any time be possible.
Having thoroughly examined the *Tārāsāra* and the *Tārānigama*,
as well as the *Mahānīla*, the *Mahācīna*, and the *Nīlatantra*, which is dear to Śiva;
The Tārākalpa, the Śaktikalpa, and likewise the Śaktisāra;
the Rudrayāmala and also the Nīlasārasvata.
The Liṅgatantra, the Yonitantra, the Ṣoḍhātantra, and the Mahāmata;
these constitute the entire essence of Tārā’s family, specifically the Ūrdhvāmnāya.
Having examined various treatises for the sake of attaining mastery over the mantra of Tārā,
I shall proclaim the secret of Tārā, which is indeed the bliss of Brahman, for the benefit [of all].
Thus ends the first auspicious invocation.

Having first examined the meanings of various scriptures, [I shall explain] the secret of the venerable Goddess Tārā, which bestows desire, wealth, and liberation through the Tārā-mantra, and which belongs to the lineage of all gurus.

For the sake of understanding the rituals such as the morning duties (*prātaḥkṛtya*) and so forth, and for the purpose of defining the deities and mantras, this text is being composed with great effort by me, Brahmānanda, for the benefit of Kahitāya. In the first Nigama-kalpa, on the island of jewels (*ratnadvīpa*), in the abode of the gods...
Having heard these words from the mouth of Kālī, Sadāśiva was not at all pleased.
Questioning her again and again, he posed this very question to Śivā:
"How was Rāvaṇa, whose face was once terrifying in form, destroyed in the past?"
The goddess Tārā, who grants boons and fearlessness, holds a sword and a severed head; she has a flickering tongue and a fierce form, and is highly honored by all.
Then the gods, filled with anxiety and having resolved upon the matter for Rudra’s sake,
arrived together with the deities to offer praise to Brahmā.
Seeing them, the Great Goddess, the bestower of liberation and the giver of the wealth of poetic talent,
was overcome with shame and drew her sword in her right hand.
With her face bowed in shame, Lambodarī stood aside;
Brahmā then took the garment that had fallen from Rudra and wore it as his skin-clothing.
Having assumed the *kāñcīmudrā* and holding a knife in his right hand,
he cast his crown upon the ground and invoked Rudra there.
Falling to the ground, the Lord of Gods fell at his feet.
"O Goddess! Twelve tens of thousands (120,000) verses of this book have been examined; I am not able to speak even a fraction [of its merit]. O Sovereign of the Gods, tell me the yoga!"
O worshipful Kālikā, O Goddess! Be gracious, O you who are affectionate toward your devotees!
Having heard the words of Śiva, Tāriṇī smiled and said:
"All men are of your form; all women are of my form."
O Mahādeva! Cultivate this yoga day by day;
then a beautiful blue lotus was placed at your lotus-feet.
Having taken it with the left hand and sprinkled it with those waters,
one should hold the drinking vessel given by Rudra in the left hand.
By this, she became Tārā, with Akṣobhya as the serpent upon her head;
he himself becomes Mahākāla in the form of Tārā throughout the three worlds.
Upon remembering her, both worldly enjoyment and liberation are immediately held in the palm of one's hand.
Such is the Great Goddess, who dwells in the void at the center of the universe;
she is the Goddess who effects creation and sustenance, whose form is the stars, and who is endowed with compassion.
And in the second, at the end of the void, she assumes the form of Suvirāj.
And in the third great void, Tārā— possessing a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning,
formless and supportless— is the accomplisher of all aims.
Relying upon the fourth void, Viṣṇu certainly protects [the world].
Born from that, the four-faced one unfailingly carries out the work of creation.
The Great Goddess, who is the form of Śiva, three-eyed, resides within the five voids;
cherished by Mahākāla, she brings the universe to dissolution.
Furthermore, for the sake of accomplishing the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa), the Great Vidyā Tāriṇī cast off her form as Kālikā at the very end and put on a garment once again.
In the sixth [chapter], Brahman consists of emptiness; likewise, the universe and the Lord of the Universe [are described].
Kālikā, who is beyond the great and great sound, is the seed-syllable that delivers one from transmigratory existence.
Tārā is situated within the five voids, and at the end of all is Kālikā.

Thus ends the chapter on the Section of Creation within the First Chapter of the *Tārārahasya*, the supreme among all secret treatises, in the dialogue between Hara and Gaurī, composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Brahmānandagirī Tīrthāvadhūta.
The practitioner, having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and partaken of food with a woman,
should face north and place his left hand upon his right hand at his navel, then [place it] on his head.

Seated within the thousand-petaled lotus in the center of the twelve-syllable lotus, white in color, adorned with various ornaments, with his left side occupied by the red Śakti, three-eyed, with bimba-red lips,
and gazing at the lotus-face of the Śakti, he is one whose mind is joyful as he beholds the Guru.

Having visualized [the deity] seated upon a svastika and having worshipped with mental offerings, one should recite "Aiṃ" one hundred and eight times; then, having offered the recitation, one should prostrate.
Oṃ, that which has the form of an unbroken circle pervades all that is moving and unmoving.
Salutation to that venerable Guru by whom that state has been revealed.
Oṃ, homage to that glorious Guru, by whom the eye was opened for one blinded by the darkness of ignorance with the probe of the collyrium of knowledge.
Having risen during the final watch of the night, one should meditate upon [it] from the aperture of Brahmā.
Maheśvara, whose form is semen, is united with the red Śakti;
he is the Guru, white as camphor, within the great thousand-petaled lotus.
Having risen during the final watch of the night, one should practice that consciousness in all branches of knowledge and in all daily duties, such as the morning rituals.
In the yoga of *dyāna*, one should hold the right hand over the left hand.

Thus, because of statements regarding morning rituals and other practices that accord with various scriptures, there is a reversal in the case of Tārā. And in the *Tārāgama*: "One should place the left hand upon one's own navel or right hand."
And one should meditate upon the venerable Guru, joined with Śakti, within the thousand-petaled lotus.

O Śiva! Even in the Mahānīla and all the Tārā vidyās, there is a transposition regarding the initial visualization and so forth; likewise, O Śiva, there is the application of the hands at one's own navel in the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and other rites.

The foremost of practitioners should meditate upon [the deity] within a thousand-petaled great lotus, possessing a radiance like that of a jasmine flower or the moon, and conjoined with the red Śakti.
And in the *Tārānigama*:
"In the morning, [one should meditate on] the Guru, white, with two eyes and two arms, upon a white lotus at the head."
The peaceful face-lotus of the Goddess, with hands granting boons and fearlessness.
Having seen that which is seen— the one composed of Brahman, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman,
and adorned with various ornaments— one should meditate upon him while seated in the svastika posture.
To the God who bestows all knowledge, whose very nature is the bliss of wisdom,
and likewise to the seed-syllable Vāgbhava for the purification of all knowledge—
whosoever would meditate upon Tāriṇī without having recited the Vāgbhava seed-syllable [is unsuccessful].
O Lord of Gods! there is no success for him, and there are obstacles in his ritual activities.
In the morning, having diligently honored the Guru upon a white lotus on the head,
one should mutter the Vāgbhava seed-syllable for the purification of all knowledge.
Having recited the seed-syllable Vāgbhava, one should prostrate again and again.
One should prostrate twice with the mantra spoken in the *Sarvasādhāraṇabrahmakhaṇḍa*.
In that regard, the performance of four rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is mandatory.
One should always prostrate to the venerable Guru while joined with these two mantras.
By means of the specific Tārā mantra and the two [mantras] spoken by the Kula.

Then, seated in the svastika posture, [one should meditate upon] Kuṇḍalinī, who is encircled by the orb of the earth with its three and a half coils, who possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns and a coolness like ten million moons, who is enveloped by the self-manifested liṅga (svayambhū-liṅga), whose nature is formless, and who consists of the Supreme Brahman.
She whose mind rejoices in the bliss of knowledge, who is the very embodiment of Mahāyoga, appearing before me from her own golden-hued head, born from a lotus grove,
consisting of the single articulated sound of many *praṇavas*, and whose nature is the ultimate reality (*tattva*).

Between the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*, in the very center of the middle of the *suṣumnā*, one should cause [the breath] to enter the *citriṇī*, the channel of Brahman (*brahmanāḍī*). Having visualized a second lotus on the left, moving with a soft and slow gait and becoming merged [with it], one should rest in the heart-lotus, contemplate the yoga of the Guru, and worship with mental offerings.
One should always meditate with devotion upon her, who is the primordial of all and has the form of a serpent;
encircling the linga within the lotus of the earth, she shines forth in the form of Brahman.
Thus it is stated in the *Śaktisāra* (p.
6), in the *Tārāsāra*, the *Rudrādhyāya*, and other such texts.

O Goddess, if one recites [the mantra] a hundred crores of times while meditating on the Self-born (Svayambhū), or on a source (yoni), or on a linga, there will indeed be no accomplishment for that person regarding Śiva.
In front of the Merudaṇḍa, threefold and endowed with qualities,
[is the Suṣumnā], situated between the Iḍā and Piṅgalā, in the very center of the middle.
One should move the supreme, dark-blue, pure energy that illuminates knowledge—
possessing the brilliance of ten million lightning flashes and as subtle as a spider's thread.
In the center, by means of the Brahma-nadi, one should bring [the disciple] who possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns;
then, in the second [position], on the left, one should lead him into the presence of the Guru with focused awareness.
There, having brought forth the supreme, pure, auspicious [power] that kindles knowledge,
which possesses the brilliance of ten million lightning flashes and whose essence is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
One should contemplate the supreme Kuṇḍalinī-śakti as possessing form;
having brought her into its center, one should visualize her as red in color.
Then one attains perfection, and not otherwise even in ten million aeons—
the perfection which consists of knowledge and bliss, and which directly bestows all happiness.
One should visualize her as richly adorned with various ornaments in the presence of the Guru;
having worshipped her mentally, one should recite the root mantra one hundred times.
Having joined his palms in reverence, he should meditate upon the Supreme Deity;
there, he should project the form of Kālī Tripurasundarī.
Having performed the morning rites, he who then mutters the root mantra [visualizes] Śivasundarī, who possesses the luster of a thousand rising suns and has two arms.
O Great Goddess, his accomplishment [is achieved] in the heart by the hosts of Yoginīs.

By this [method], having visualized Kuṇḍalinī in her embodied form in the presence of the Guru, having worshipped her mentally, and having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times, one should conclude by prostrating. Then, having prostrated on the ground and looked upon a young girl and Brāhmaṇas, one should recite [the following].
Oṃ. I am the deity and none other; I am Brahman alone, not subject to sorrow.
I am of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss, possessing an eternally liberated essence.
Supreme bliss beyond the bliss of Brahman, the bestower of knowledge,
the Tāraka devotee, the bliss-filled bliss itself— He is Sadāśiva.
I am Bhairava; I am rich in nectar; I am the knower of reality; I belong to the Kula women;
I possess the grace of the Guru; and I am a servant of the practitioner of Śakti.
Ratānanda, Kulānanda, and Kumārīdāsa,
as well as I, Kumārīvaṇik, and Tārācaraṇanāyaka.
Having recited this as spoken in the *Tārānigama*, one should go outside.
O Goddess Śivā, without the morning rites, no accomplishment (*siddhi*) arises.
One certainly does not obtain the fruit of worship through the mere recitation of mantras.
All ritual action— whether Vedic or Tantric— would be fruitless for one who is devoid of the morning rites, just as any rite performed without purity is fruitless.

Thus ends the first chapter, concerning the morning rites and so forth, in the *Tārārahasya*, the supreme among all secret treatises, within the dialogue between Hara and Gaurī, composed by the venerable Kulāvadhūta, the Lord of Tīrtha Brahmānandagiri, a wandering ascetic (parivrājaka) and teacher (ācārya) of the Paramahaṃsa order.

Then, following the morning rites (*prātaḥkṛtya*), there is the bath. For practitioners, the ritual actions—both Vedic and Tantric—should be described as extending from the time of dawn until the end of the *mahāniśā* (the deep night). However, because the worship of Śiva involves the unification of the Vedic and Tantric traditions, his worship is also included. Therefore, [one should perform this] at a river or similar location.

Having gone there and performed ablution, one should make the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "Oṃ, beginning with 'today' (*adya*) and so forth, for the pleasure of the venerable goddess Tārā, I shall perform my bath in this water," and then draw a triangle in the water. Thus it is said in the *Tārānigama*:
For the pleasure of the Goddess, those who know the Tantras should perform a ritual bath;
having invoked the sacred waters (tīrtha) into the water and performed the recitation (japa), they should first immerse themselves.
And in that very same Rudrayāmala (p. 8):
"Wherever the Mahāvidyā is worshipped by practitioners, there a downward-facing triangle is prescribed."
In the triangle of the gods, it should be performed facing upwards, as approved by the ritual injunctions.
In this regard: O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī,
Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, please be present in these waters.
Thus, having invoked the *tīrtha* from the solar disc by means of the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*, performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*),
and assigned [the mantras] to the hands, limbs, and six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), one should contemplate the form of the Goddess; having visualized oneself as consisting of Tārā,
one should recite the root mantra ten times on the head, ten times at the heart, and ten times in the water.
Having drawn a triangle, a circle, and a square, and having displayed the *dhenu*, *yoni*, *matsya*, and *aṅkuśa* mudrās,

one should pour water twelve times facing the sun and sprinkle the head seven times with the root mantra (*mūla*). Then, facing upward, [one should use] the water flowing from the feet of the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*).
One should bathe. Having invoked the holy ford (tīrtha) from the ocean of stars and other sources into the water, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga).
One should meditate upon oneself in the water as having the form of the Goddess, consisting of Tāriṇī.
Having recited the root mantra ten times over the head, the heart, and the water,
the wise practitioner should draw a triangle, a circle, and a square within the water.
One should display the goad, the cow-seal (dhenumudrā), the womb-seal (yoni), and the fish-seal.
Having offered water to the Sun, one should sprinkle the head seven times. Thus is the ritual bath.
And likewise, in the Mahācīna-mahātārārṇava and other texts:
One should perform the Vedic bath, and immediately thereafter the Tantric one;
having performed the Vedic twilight prayer (saṃdhyā), one should personally perform the Tantric one.
Having drawn a triangle in the water, one should then invoke the sacred fords (tīrthas);
having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with the essence-mantra ending with the wife of fire (the *svāhā* mantra).
The practitioner should offer water with its roots intact upon the head;
thereafter, the best of practitioners should offer it seven times upon the ground.
Having taken water in the left hand and covering it with the right,
one should recite the mantra three times and then recite the five syllables.
The syllable *kṣāṃ* joined with the moon, as well as the first of the seven colors;
then the seed-syllable of fire, of earth, and immediately after that, the one of water.
Ha, Ya, Va, La, Ra—these constitute the Aghamarṣaṇa mantra within the Ekajaṭā mantra.
One should bathe the head with drops of dripping water using the mudrā;
indeed, that mudrā is the Tattvamudrā, used during the twilight rites for the libation to the Kula.
Sprinkling that water with his right hand while directing it through the left channel (vāmanāḍī),
he should [perform this] before a stone or diamond using the Astra-bīja mantra.
The practitioner should strike [the target] for the sake of all accomplishments and the accomplishment of knowledge,
while meditating on black-colored water and upon the person together with their sin.
Having performed the cleansing of the channels and likewise the washing of the body,
one should then offer libations to the Goddess, whose nature is the bliss of nectar.
[One should worship] the gods, the ṛṣis, and the ancestors, then the guru, the supreme guru (paraguru),
then the higher and lower guru (parāparaguru), and then the supreme guru (parameṣṭhiguru). Then, having uttered the root [mantra], [one worships] the goddess Tārā thereafter.
Afterwards, I shall then offer libations to the illustrious Ekajaṭā.
To the one endowed with the power of illumination, I offer this arghya.
Having meditated upon Tārā and likewise Ekajaṭā within the orb of the sun,
one should offer three *arghya* oblations accompanied by flowers while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra.
Then one should meditate upon the Gāyatrī and recite it twenty times.

Having drawn a downward-facing triangle in the water, having invoked the sacred waters (*tīrtha*) with the mantra beginning "Oṃ Gaṅge ca," and having displayed the *yonimudrā*, one should perform the ritual sipping (*ācamana*) with the root mantra and a blade of *kuśa* grass while reciting: "Oṃ, svāhā to the principle of the self (*ātmatattva*);
Oṃ, svāhā to the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*); Oṃ, svāhā to the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*). Then, with the root mantra and the *kuśa* grass...

Having sprinkled water seven times on the head and seven times on the ground, taking water in the left hand and covering it with the right hand, one should meditate upon the water as being of the nature of light, recite the root mantra three times over it, consecrate it three times with "haṃ yaṃ vaṃ laṃ raṃ," and [sprinkle] with the dripping drops of water.

Having sprinkled the head seven times with the *tattvamudrā*, one takes the remaining water with the right hand, draws it in through the *iḍā* [nāḍī], and washes the state within the body; then, visualizing that water as black in color, [one expels it] along with the personification of sin (*pāpapuruṣa*) situated in the left side of the abdomen. (p. 10)

One should strike the previously prepared vajra-stone with the syllable *phaṭ*. Then, having washed one's hands and recollected Tārā, one should offer libations with each handful [of water], saying: *oṃ devāṃs tarpayāmi*, *oṃ ṛṣīṃs tarpayāmi*, *oṃ pitṝṃs tarpayāmi*, *oṃ gurūṃs tarpayāmi*, *oṃ paramagurūṃs tarpayāmi*, *oṃ*...
I satisfy the supreme and subordinate gurus; *oṃ*, I satisfy the supreme teachers (*parameṣṭhi-guru*).
Reciting the root mantra, [one says]: "I satisfy the goddess Tārā, the illustrious Ekajaṭā, svāhā"—thus three times.
Then, taking the *arghya* offering together with *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and red flowers, [one recites]: *oṃ hrīṃ haṃ saḥ*.
"Obeisance to the glorious Sūrya accompanied by the power of light; I offer this *arghya*.

Having thus offered the *arghya* to the Sun and meditated upon the Goddess within the solar orb, one should recite the *Gāyatrī* and [offer it] to the venerable Ekajaṭā, the Goddess Tārā residing in the solar orb.
"This is the arghya; salutations," [recite] three times. Then, with palms joined in reverence:

"Oṃ! In the morning, upon the lotus of the support (ādhāra-kamala) above the circle of fire (hutabhuṅ-maṇḍala), I contemplate that Vidyā in the form of the seed-syllable of speech (vāg-bīja), radiant as a mass of lightning."
Her hands are beautifully adorned with a flower, a bow of sugarcane, a noose, and a goad;
she assumes a body according to her own will, and her nature consists of the Great Knowledge (Guruvidyā).
At midday, within the solar mandala at the pericarp of the heart-lotus,
one should meditate upon the Goddess, whose essence is the seed-syllable Kāma and who is as red as liquid lac.
She is endowed with a flower, a young *puṇḍra* fruit, a sugarcane bow, a noose, and a goad;
she is surrounded by the principal [energies] and served by the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*).
In the sacrificial rite, [one should meditate on] her who possesses the luster of the moon, seated upon a lotus in the moon,
whose essence is the seed-syllable of Śakti, and who is equipped with a bow, arrows, a noose, and a goad.
Having meditated upon the Blessed Lady, who is eternally surrounded by her retinue,
whose form consists of the syllables of the eternal Yugas, and who resembles the finest bell.
Therefore, one should meditate on Tārāsāra as Gāyatrī within the Tārakāmaṇi,
and especially upon the goddess Tripurā within the Ekajaṭāmaṇi.
This is because it is stated thus in the *Tārāsāra*: "And this is the meditation (*dhyāna*) upon Gāyatrī in relation to Tripurāsundarī. Likewise, in the *Nīlasarasvatītantra* and the *Tārānigama*:
"Having uttered the word 'To Tārā,' immediately thereafter [one says] 'vidmahe'..."
Then one should offer to Mahogrā, and after that, the mantra "dhīmahi."
Having uttered "tanno devī," one should then offer [the oblation] with "pracodayāt."
"Oṃ, may we know Tārā; may we meditate upon Mahogrā; may the Goddess impel us.
This Gāyatrī, which is approved by various texts such as the *Tārānigama*, should be recited.
Having first recited the common [Gāyatrī], the best of practitioners should then recite it ten times.
One should recite the Gāyatrī, the distinguished vidyā that bestows all accomplishments.
The foremost of practitioners who recites [the mantra] either a hundred or even twenty times shall be liberated from all sins and dwell personally in the city of Tārā.
The man who is a killer of cows, ungrateful, a slayer of Brahmins or women,
one who violates the teacher's bed, or even one who is lustful toward his daughter-in-law;
One shall be liberated from these sins; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Sadāśiva! No sin greater than approaching a maiden has ever existed, nor shall there ever be one.
Furthermore, the world is liberated even by the mere recollection of the Gāyatrī,
or even by a hundred-fold repetition of the Gāyatrī as declared in the Āgamas.
One shall be liberated from these sins; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Lord of the Gods!
And one is liberated from these sins even through the recollection of this specific [text].
Therefore, this proclaimed Vidyā should be recited by one desiring success:
having first extracted the Kūrca-bīja (HŪM), then [the name] Bhagavatī Ekajaṭā,
followed by "vidmahe," then "ghoradaṃṣṭre," and after that, "dhīmahi."
Having recited that [mantra] for us, O Tārā, one should then proceed with the prose passage.
Having recited "Oṃ, O Blessed One Ekajaṭā, we know; we meditate on the one with terrible fangs;
may she, Tārā, impel us" either one hundred or twenty times, and having offered [the merit], he should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
If one recites the Gāyatrī but does not then recite the root mantra,
that twilight rite should be known as fruitless and is fit only for malevolent magic.
One who omits the morning twilight prayer shall not obtain the fruit of bathing;
and one who omits the midday twilight prayer shall not attain the fruit of worship.
For one who omits the evening twilight devotion, there shall always be an obstacle to the recitation of mantras.
Therefore, O beautiful one, one who knows the truth should perform the three twilight devotions.
One should not perform the libation (tarpaṇa) in the morning, nor especially in the evening;
by performing the libation at midday, one shall obtain the fruit as described.
A twilight prayer (saṃdhyā) performed without the water-offering (arghya) is considered to bestow sorrow and suffering;
the arghya must be offered at all three junctions of the day, otherwise the recitation (japa) is fruitless.
And Gāyatrī, along with her mantra, is truly, truly [powerful], O fair-faced one!

Then, by means of the *saṃhāramudrā*, one should lead that radiance into one’s own heart; having prostrated, one should perform worship. Thus is the twilight rite (*sandhyā*) concerning the venerable Ekajaṭā. Now follows the twilight rite of Ugratārā.

Having offered water three times to the deity with the root mantra, take water in the left hand and perform the covering as before. Then perform the *aghamarṣaṇa* and likewise the sipping of water (*ācamana*).
Then, reciting the root mantra, say three times: "I satisfy the venerable goddess Ugratārā; obeisance. Then:

Oṃ hrīṃ haṃ saḥ, this arghya to the glorious Sūrya, obeisance! Thus, with the Gāyatrī mantra, [one offers] "this arghya to the glorious Ugratārā residing in the solar disc, obeisance," three times. Then, one should meditate upon the Gāyatrī.
O fair-faced one, having offered water three times with the root mantra to the deity,
the supreme *aghamarṣaṇa* rite should then be performed by the Goddess.
Then, having offered praise, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana); thereafter follows the libation to the desired deities (iṣṭatarpaṇa).
Having offered the respectful oblation (arghya) with the Gāyatrī mantra, the practitioner should perform meditation.
When the deities are gratified, the lineages of gurus become satisfied;
therefore, within the body of this Goddess, there exist eternal rajasas.
And here, the meditation common to all brings about all victories,
because Tāriṇī consists of all the gods and is composed of the three qualities.

In the morning, one should meditate upon Brāhmī in a starry sky— she who possesses the luster of a thousand rising suns, whose lotus-like hands hold a book and a rosary, and who is clothed in a black antelope skin.
At midday,
[one should meditate on] the goddess of dark complexion, with four arms, her hands shining with the conch and discus,
bearing a mace and a lotus, and seated upon the solar throne.
Then, in the evening, one should meditate upon the boon-granting goddess Gāyatrī—
white-complexioned, clad in white garments, and seated upon the bull-throne.
Meditating upon the Goddess— three-eyed, bestowing boons, holding a noose, a skull-cup, and a trident, and seated in the center of the solar disc— one should practice her worship.
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Lajjā, one should then take the word Ugratārā in the vocative case,
O Queen of Gods, followed immediately by "vidmahe."
Then follow the words "śmaśānavāsini dhīmahi," after which "tannaḥ tāre" is extracted, and then the word "pracodayāt."
O Goddess of Gods! [The mantra] ending with the vocative case, followed by "pracodayāt," should then follow.
"Hrīṃ! We know Ugratārā; we meditate upon her who dwells in the cremation ground; may she, Tārā, inspire us.
Then, having recited the common Gāyatrī ten times and completed it,

One should recite the Viśeṣagāyatrī one hundred and eight times. Then, with the *saṃhāramudrā*, one should draw that radiance into one’s own heart. This is the twilight ritual (*saṃdhyā*) of Ugratārā.
Having purified the water with the root mantra and having recited it five times while facing the sun, [one should offer it].
Having offered water five times and sipped water with *oṃ hrīṃ svāhā*, one should join the palms in reverence and recite:
"Oṃ! To the Goddess who dwells in the midst of the cremation ground, who bestows the four aims of human life, who possesses the luster of a great cloud, and who shines upon a blue lotus."
Richly adorned with the splendor of all ornaments, she took her eye from the eye of Hara.

Having recited this, one should draw a hexagon in the water, invoke the sacred waters (*tīrtha*), perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) with the *tattva-mantra*, and offer water three times on the ground while reciting the root mantra; this is the *aghamarṣaṇa*.
Then, having performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*) as in the case of Ekajaṭā, one should present the *arghya* offering.
Having purified the root mantra fivefold at the base of the water,
and having offered the water five times, one should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) as in the worship.
Having meditated upon the Goddess within the orb of the sun, the practitioner should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana);
thereafter, the practitioner should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyā) according to the method of Ekajaṭā.

For the *arghya* offering, [recite] with the *gāyatrī*: "To the Goddess Tārā, who resides within the solar orb, the venerable Śrī Nīlasarasvatī—this *arghya*, svāhā! Thus three times. Then, the meditation (*dhyāna*) for the morning.
The goddess born from the lotus has four faces and two eyes, possesses two arms, is adorned with a necklace of pearls, and is joined to the solar disc.
At midday, one should worship Bhairavī in the form of Viṣṇu, having four arms,
adorned with pearls and rubies, and beautified by various kinds of food and offerings.
To the Goddess Gāyatrī, the bestower of mantra-siddhi, [I bow] for the sake of the foremost of practitioners.
In the evening, he beheld the five-faced, three-eyed Māheśvarī, the sustainer of the sun,
the mother of the world, and the protector of all moving beings.
First, having extracted the syllable *Tāraṃ* (Oṃ), one should join the phrase "Nīlasarasvatī" and first apply "dhīmahi," followed by "sāradāyai ca vidmahe."
Having uttered "tat naḥ śivaṃ padaṃ," one should then recite "pracodayāt."
"Oṃ, we meditate upon Nīlasarasvatī; may we know Sāradā; may she, the Auspicious One, inspire us"—with this Gāyatrī, one should recite [the mantra] according to one's capacity.
Thereafter, everything is as in the case of Ekajaṭā. However, there is a specific distinction regarding the Tārārṇava and the Mahācīna [tantras].
For women, for Śūdras, and for Brāhmaṇas, each separately,
whatever has been stated in the book must indeed be performed by the Brāhmaṇa.
Otherwise, one should know that all ritual actions such as worship and the rest are fruitless;
likewise for the morning duties, the bath, and the three daily junctures (sandhyās), O Śiva.

For women and Śūdras, the seed-syllable of modesty (*lajjābīja*) is prescribed for the *tāra* mantra; where there is the *svāhā* mantra, there *namaḥ* is prescribed. (p. 15) In all cases, such as worship, fire-oblation (*homa*), and so forth, the rule is considered to be without distinction.
Thus ends the twilight rite (saṃdhyā) of Nīlasarasvatī. Next, O Sadāśivā, I shall declare the mantra of the Goddess Tārā,
by the mere knowledge of which a man becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
Now, in the *Bījakoṣa*, the *Mahānīlatārānigama*, and other texts: "The letter *bra* (ब्र), joined with the earth (*la*), the left eye (*i*), and the lunar drop (*bindu*),
is declared to be the seed-syllable of Kāma, which bestows victory over the three worlds."
The left eye joined with the letter *kṣa*, the letter *ra*,
and the moon is known as the seed-syllable of *Lajjā* (Hrīṃ), which bestows all accomplishments.
The letter *ha*, endowed with the sixth vowel and marked by a crescent moon,
is renowned as the *kūrca* seed-syllable, famous throughout the three worlds.
The second letter of the *pavarga* and the first letter of the *ṭavarga*—
this mantra, known as the seed-syllable of the horse (*asvabīja*), is proclaimed to be the performer of all protection.
Accompanied by the crescent moon and uttered with the twelve vowels,
that is to be known as the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], which bestows the perfection of speech.
O Goddess, the thirteenth vowel, adorned with the crescent moon, is called the *tāra* and the *praṇava*; it is the very essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
The letter *ha* joined with the fifth vowel is the seed-syllable of the armor (*varma*).
Joined with the drops of water and fire (the letters *ja* and *ra*) and endowed with the fourteenth vowel (*au*),
this is declared to be the *aṅkuśa* seed-syllable, which brings auspiciousness to the three worlds.
The heart-seed (hṛdbīja) is proclaimed to begin with the letter *na* and end with the *visarga*.
The letter preceding *ha* (i.e., *sa*), joined with the second vowel (*i*),
followed by its final letter (*kṣa*) and the letter *ha*, combined with the wife of fire (*svāhā*).
The syllable "brahmāgni" (ha), ending with the left eye (i) and joined with the king of the twice-born (u), is known as the seed-syllable of the bride; it is like a bride, O illustrious one.
"You are a child, you are worthy of salutation, you are a servant, and you are indeed a teacher.
A mother should never conceal anything from her children."
Therefore, O Lord, O Great God, please tell that Tārā-mantra, which is difficult for even gods to obtain and which bestows the eightfold supernatural powers (vasu-siddhi), to those who ask me.
Kālī, Tārā, Mahāvidyā, Ṣoḍaśī,
Bhuvaneśvarī, Bhairavī, Chinnamastā, Mātaṅgī, Kamalātmikā, Dhūmāvatī, and Vagalā are proclaimed as the Mahāvidyās.
Merely by hearing these, one shall become a master of all supernatural attainments (siddhis).
Due to the distinctions between Viṣṇu-vidyā, Deva-vidyā, and Śiva-vidyā,
as well as through the various divisions of Śakti-vidyā, many types of Vidyā have been proclaimed.
From the beginning of the Satya Yuga until the end of the three ages, Vidyā remains eternally awake;
in the Kali age, Kālī awakens, and in the Kali age she remains eternally awake.
In the Kali age there is Kālī, in the Kali age there is Kṛṣṇa, and in the Kali age there is Gopālakālikā.
Kālī and Tārā are the Great Vidyās who bestow great accomplishments;
in all the Great Vidyās, their perfection is unsurpassed in the Kali age.
O Goddess, composed of all knowledge! In the Kali age, there is unsurpassed accomplishment [through you]. Kālikā is the saving Vidyā, saluted by all the Āmnāyas.
By the mere sacrifice to those two, Sadāśiva himself becomes directly accomplished.
Just as Kālī, so too Tārā and Nīlasarasvatī;
likewise Tripurasundarī shall grant the fruit of all desired objects.
Whatever man might accomplish by relying on the doctrine of non-duality, he shall be honored throughout the three worlds; he is indeed the very son of Tārā.
But that mantra-practitioner who, having made a distinction, performs the practice here—O Goddess, there is no atonement for him; indeed, he is cooked in hell.
By the very practice of these [mantras], fame and accomplishment are attained eternally;
by relying solely on devotion, one shall hold the four aims of human life in the palm of one's hand.
And Tripurā is the Great Vidyā who bestows the accomplishment of many means of practice;
by whose grace, through the mantra, both worldly enjoyment and liberation arise.
The Kālikā Tārakā Vidyā bestows the abundance of spiritual powers in the Kali age;
consisting of the practice of vigilance, she becomes propitious without hardship in the Kali age.
Nor is there such a profusion of ritual applications in the case of the Net of Deposits (nyāsajāla) and so forth;
nor would the conduct of a bound soul (paśu) be appropriate therein. Therefore, that [latter] means of accomplishment is auspicious.
O Goddess, the sādhanā of Kālikā for my sake shines forth in the worship of Kālikā;
having awakened to that very [truth], one should perform the sādhanā.
This is her second form, which is established at the root of creation;
and the means for its accomplishment bestows all spiritual attainments.
Wealth, grain, a virtuous son, a wife, enjoyments, and likewise liberation—
one obtains these without delay merely by the recollection of her speech.
Without having studied the treatises on prosody, even for a poet,
speech consisting of prose and verse does not issue from his mouth.
Atomicity, lightness, pervasiveness, radiance, and likewise magnanimity;
invisibility, the form of grossness, and the solidification of fire and water.
He is the pervasive Lord himself who paralyzes the moon, the sun, fire, and the elements;
he possesses the accomplishment of mantras as well as the attainments of the Purāṇas and Āgamas.
One should bring the king’s wife under one's influence through a specific mode of courtship;
by means of the sixty-four arts, the accomplishment of traveling through the sky is attained.
Tārā resides in the five voids, and Kālikā resides at the end of all; wherever the siddhis are located, they are brought there and bestowed.
O Goddess! if it can be accomplished amidst the host of Tārakas, then one attains perfection at all times within the Kula-maṇḍala.
For one who is devoid of the conduct of his family, there is neither spiritual accomplishment nor a happy rebirth.
The slayer of a Brahmin, the ungrateful person, he who has gone to the wife of his guru,
he who has gone to a maiden, he who has gone to a daughter-in-law, he who has gone to a Brāhmaṇa woman, and he who has gone to a cow.
One who harms all living beings, especially Brahmins;
one who causes the emission of semen upon the earth; and one who is averse to the worship of Śiva.
Listen, O child Mahādeva! Just as one who has committed great sins is liberated from them, O Lord, if the Tārā mantra is heard.
He is completely liberated from all sins, even if he was previously joined with every sin.
For one who is devoid of the family initiation (kuladīkṣā), there is neither spiritual accomplishment nor a favorable rebirth;
therefore, with every effort, a man should become a teacher of Tārā.
If one is devoid of the conduct of his family, he is overtaken by all sins.
For one who delights in the family tradition and constantly propitiates the family deity— the venerable goddess Tārakā— success rests within his very hand.
He who possesses knowledge of proper conduct but fails to perform the duties of his family is cooked in a terrible hell for even hundreds of millions of kalpas.
And that man who is devoted to another's wife and who stands in the midst of a [Buddhist] wheel shall become a worm in the excrement of a female dog and remain so on earth for ten thousand kalpas.
And having obtained the means of accomplishment, one may take pleasure in the wives of others.
Having abandoned the mother’s womb, he may wander through all wombs;
the best of practitioners should be free from transformation and free from conceptual construction.

The term *mātṛpada* refers to the seven Mothers; this was understood by the true guru Siddhānandagiri through the study of the Tārā-nigama and other scriptures. Indeed, he is capable of bestowing his own wife, who is devotedly affectionate toward her devotees.
Then, having brought a woman, one will certainly accomplish [the rite] for others.
That very best of practitioners, being certain regarding the non-conceptual state, should be bestowed upon other practitioners; then another [disciple] is accepted.
He who is devoted to the gods, but unable to give his own wife,
should instead bring a female dancer and accomplish the practice of the Śakti.
If a practitioner offers his own wife in the midst of the wheel,
I dwell upon his head, along with the gurus and the practitioners.
O God! All accomplishments are within the range of his vision.
Thus begins the section from the *Tārānigama* up to the end of the *Cīna* [tantras].
Now, the Vidyā will be explained:
she is eternally *Tārā* because she delivers [beings] from the differentiation and fragmentation of that [reality].
In the first kalpa, Rudra himself was Ekajaṭa with disheveled hair;
for this reason she is called Ekajaṭā, and her mantra is now described.
Since the knowledge propitiated by Vasiṣṭha does not yield fruit quickly,
for that reason even that sage bestowed a most terrible curse.
From that time forward, this vidyā has not granted its fruit to anyone.
That was extracted by that very Śiva himself, acting as the Guru.

The seed-syllable of modesty (LĀM), the seed-syllable of the bride (HRĪM), and thereafter the seed-syllable of the tuft (KŪRCAM), ending with the weapon-mantra (PHAṬ); this is proclaimed as having the nature of five rays of light.
Thus, this Ekajaṭā-vidyā is concealed within all scriptures;
yet it is present throughout all scriptures as the passionate goddess who bestows accomplishment.
O Goddess, if a human being on earth is burdened by a hundred thousand great sins,
he will certainly become liberated while living simply by hearing this.
The venerable Tārā must never be given away on earth, in heaven, or in the subterranean realm;
if the Goddess is bestowed [in marriage], one will certainly be cooked in hell.

If a Śūdra, fallen under the sway of delusion, should desire the auspicious Tārakā and other Great Vidyās for his eldest son— who is peaceful and endowed with the knowledge of his own true nature— his downfall is certain.
And for women as well, O lady of excellent hips! it is indeed always forbidden.
First, Śrī Ekajaṭā was extracted; thereafter, Śrī Tārā was not mentioned because of the hearing of faults [associated with her] everywhere and because of its being one's own dharma.
When the Vidyā begins with the Śrī-bīja, then Śrī is present in every direction.
When the Vidyā, beginning with Vāgbhava, bestows the state of mastery over speech,
and if, by good fortune, this Great Vidyā of five rays is obtained;
O Śaṅkara! both his worldly enjoyment and liberation are indeed held in the palm of his hand.
This is the *śaktisiddhi* mantra of the goddess Ekajaṭā. Preceded by the syllable of modesty (*lajjā*), this other mantra bestows both enjoyment and liberation;
it consists of five and a half syllables and grants great supernatural attainments (*mahāsiddhi*).
The Gāyatrī of this [Tārā] is:
"Oṃ, may we know Tārā; may we meditate upon her who grants liberation; may she, Nīlā, inspire us. Thus is the Gāyatrī of the Tārā mantra.
Kāmākhyā is another Vidyā, proclaimed as Kāmatārā;
she is the Goddess who bestows both enjoyment and liberation, worshipped in all the scriptures.

Thus ends the mantra of Kāmatārā. Her Gāyatrī is found in that same source: "Oṃ, we know her who is called Kāmā; we meditate upon her who belongs to the Kulakaula; may she, the Dark One (Śyāmā), inspire us. This is the variety known as Ekajaṭā. Now follows Ugratārā.
The Vidyā known on the surface of the earth as Kūrcā and others, consisting of five rays,
is proclaimed as Ugratārā in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld.
By remembering her, one is immediately liberated from all sins;
she is the goddess who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, worshipped in all tantras.
The Gāyatrī for her is as follows: *Oṃ ugratāre dhīmahi, siddhisāre vidmahe, tanno nīle pracodayāt*. This is the Ugratārā Gāyatrī.
The mantra for that same [deity] is as follows:
Then follows the *badhūla* and the *kūrca*; this great mantra ends with the weapon (*astra*).
She is proclaimed as the consort of Śambhu, kept secret in all tantras.
The *gāyatrī* for this [mantra] is found in that very same place: "Oṃ, we meditate upon the wife of Śambhu; we contemplate the Great Fierce One; may Tārā impel us.
First [one places] the *kūrca*, then the *lajjā*, and after that the *badhū* seed-syllable.
The great mantra ending in *phaṭ* brings auspiciousness to all tantras.
The Goddess, beloved of Mahākāla, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
*Hūṃ hrīṃ strīṃ phaṭ*. Her *gāyatrī* is: *Oṃ tārakāyai vidmahe*.
"Let us meditate upon the beloved of Mahākāla; may that Śakti inspire us.
Thus ends the Gāyatrī mantra of Mahākālapriyā. Now begins the section on Nīlasarasvatī.
The mantra of Ekajaṭā, beginning with "Tārā," is proclaimed as that of Nīlavāṇī;
by the proper recollection of which one will certainly attain mastery over speech.
The Gāyatrī for this [mantra] is: "Oṃ, let us know Nīlasarasvatī; let us meditate upon Śrītārā; may that goddess inspire us."
Ekajaṭā, beginning with Vāgbhava, is Mahānīlasarasvatī;
by the mere remembrance of her, one immediately becomes a master of all supernatural attainments (siddhis).
This is the Gāyatrī of this [deity]. It was written during the third twilight; the Gāyatrī of Ugratārā was heard during the twilight.
Now begins the section on the *kullukā*.

The *kullukā* is the knowledge-mantra (*vidyā-mantra*). In every application, Padmāvatī is also [to be used]. The application of the *lajjā*, *badhū*, and *kūrca* seed-syllables bestows accomplishment (*siddhi*).
This Kullukā has been fully explained; it is kept secret in all the tantras.
Having first extracted the Praṇava, then the word "Padme" twice,
having uttered the word "Mahāpadme," and then the word "Padmāvati," followed by "Māye Svāhā"— this application of the great mantra bestows success.

Oṃ padme padme mahāpadme padmāvati! śrīṃ hrīṃ svāhā. Since it is heard in this scripture [the *Māyātantra*] that "māyā" [is used], two instances of the word for modesty (*lajjā*) are to be understood. Those who claim that the word "māyā" ends in a vocative are barbarians (*mleccha*). [As stated] in the *Tārānigama*:
In the *Padmāvatī-prakaraṇa*: Oṃ, Padme, and again Padme, then Mahāpadme;
thereafter, Padmāvati, then the two *lajjās*, and then Svāhā—this is the mantra.
Because she delivers [beings], Kālī is certainly determined to be Tārā herself;
moreover, her many mantras exist within all the tantras, āgamas, and so forth.
The Mahāvidyās, perfected through Śakti, are remembered as the essence of essences;
there is no mantra on earth that bestows such accomplishment as these eight Vidyās.
Of all these mantras, three deities are traditionally taught:
the first is said to be Ekajaṭā, the second is Ugratārā, and the third is Nīlavāṇī; she is considered the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Therein, the single characteristic of the extraction of the Ekajaṭā mantra has been written in brief:
because she is the fierce destroyer of calamities, she is celebrated as Ugratārā;
because speech was bestowed by Nīlā, she is therefore Nīlasarasvatī.

Regarding the reading of the letter *la* in the word *nīlayā*, it does not mean that [the goddess] becomes Nīlasarasvatī at that time; rather, those who say so are mistaken. O practitioner! These are the seers (*ṛṣi*) and meters (*chandas*) of these eight mantras.
Listen, and I shall here proclaim a secret that is approved by me.
Having observed the blue conduct (nīlācāra) and so forth, as well as the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa),
I shall explain each one individually, along with the eight mantras for the Tāraka.
Akṣobhya is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), and Vṛhatī is its meter (chandas);
the seed-syllable (bīja) is said to be the mantra of Lajjā, and Kūrca is proclaimed as its power (śakti).

Residing in the forest on fruits and roots, one should recite the mantra— one hundred thousand times— consisting of the *kīlaka*, one’s own seed-syllable (*bīja*), and the well-perfected seed-syllable of the bride (*badhū*).
At night, his mouth filled with betel-leaf, he delights in union with the Śakti within the Kula.
In that regard, Śiva has elaborated upon the delight in the bliss of Brahman;
one should offer oblations with blue lotuses and with the threefold sweet [substances].
This procedure applies to the primary mantra, to its variations, and to all phonemes.

O child! This is the procedure for the two [forms of] Ugratārā; of this there is no doubt. And in the case of their division during the preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*), it is two hundred thousand [recitations].
In the Nīla-kalpa, within the Nīlavāṇī which is endowed with various divisions of mantras, one should recite the mantra two hundred thousand times; then, unsurpassed accomplishment is attained.
In all the *tārā* vidyās, during the preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*), one should perform oblations with blue lotuses; in their absence, with *vilva* leaves.
Know that in every case— the seer, the meter, the seed-syllable, the power, and the pin—
are distinct according to the specific division of each name-mantra.
In the practice of the Tārā mantra,
having abandoned the family born of Śakti as described in the secret teachings on the Heroic State (vīrabhāva), one shall attain the form with attributes (sākāra).
Having gathered the Śaiva doctrine as it is circulated in the Nigamas and Āgamas,

I have indeed set down in this work the worship of Tārā, the procedure for recitation (*japa*), the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and likewise the libation (*tarpaṇa*), while keeping in mind the words of Tārā herself.
Here dwells Kamalā with her palms joined in reverence, and Sāradā holding a lute.

Thus ends the chapter on Creation and so forth, in the first chapter of the *Tārārahasya*, a dialogue between Hara and Gaurī, composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Brahmānandagiri Tīrtha Svāmikulāvadhūta.
Now begins the second chapter.

In the *Tārānigama* and other texts, as well as at the root of the *Kāmākhyā*, it is stated regarding the bestowal of the *Kālī-Tārā* mantra: "He who performs contemplation upon the *cakra* during the transmission of the *Kālī-Tārā* mantra..."
One who obstructs the discourse on longevity, knowledge, and liberation shall become a worm in excrement, afflicted by colic.
O Lord! if the Tārā-vidyā is obtained by the power of fortune, one attains the fulfillment of all desires; what then to speak of liberation and the eight supernatural powers?
If the Guru in the mantra were directly Hara himself in all the Tantras,
he would never say that he could not bestow the saving Vidyā, nor would he ever refuse to give it.
(24) "O child! If, by the power of fortune and through the strength of penance accumulated over ten million births,
one should obtain the Tāraka-vidyā, he shall become a wish-fulfilling tree."
O Sadāśiva, the Tārā mantra is to be kept strictly secret;
so too are the yantra, the mantra-text, the chapter, the hymn, and the armor-verse.
The secret, the Guhyashodha, and the Tarānigama itself must be concealed with great effort;
one should never reveal the Tarā.
He who is devoted to his family's traditional occupations but is devoid of the true nature of a sentient being,
yet maintains a heroic disposition toward the mantra, the tantra, the guru, the brahmin, and the creeper;
Never to such a deceitful Kaula who bestows a boon upon him,
the giver [is punished] by the command of Śiva;
for such a man is somewhere driven by greed for wealth, greed for desire, or greed for ritual action.
If one gives [it away], O Goddess of gods, he certainly falls into hell;
he who destroys Śiva becomes a slayer of Śakti and a slayer of Brahman in the three worlds.
He alone is fallen among the Kaulas; who else on this earth is fallen?
[This applies] to one of noble birth, great aspiration, and devoted to faith and devotion.
O Wielder of the Trident! This should indeed be given to those who serve the Kaula tradition, who delight in serving Śakti, who are devoted to Tārā, who are disciplined, and who are ever-blissful;
otherwise, one would meet with death.

Having personally obtained a true Guru who is endowed with the auspicious marks, one who is likewise possessed of those marks himself, initiation must be performed; otherwise, the ritual act is fruitless.
At the root of a bilva tree, in a cremation ground, on a mountain, or on a riverbank;
in the house of the guru, at a great pīṭha, at a siddhi-pīṭha, or in a temple of Śiva.
In a solitary linga, or by a pond, or in a Shiva temple devoid of a bull,
the practitioner of mantra should always perform initiation and likewise carry out the recitation of mantras.
Where one does not see another linga within a distance of five krośas,
that is declared to be an "ekalinga" (solitary linga), which bestows the attainment of mantra-siddhi.
"O Goddess! If, by the power of fortune, the bank of the Gaṅgā is obtained,
and if initiation is performed there, it yields merit multiplied ten millionfold."
[One should avoid] the initiation of an ascetic, the initiation of one's father, the initiation of one's maternal grandfather,
that of a younger brother, and that of one who has taken the side of an enemy.
One who dwells in a secluded hermitage should never undergo initiation.
A husband shall not initiate his wife; a father shall not initiate his daughter;
likewise, an elder brother shall not initiate his younger brother.
On the third day of the initiation (dīkṣā), having performed the auspicious rites such as shaving the hair,
one should consume sacrificial food (haviṣya) on that day and observe a fast on the following day.
Having received the command of the guru, one should personally fetch flowers and other offerings;
having established five jars, one should worship the deities therein.
In the first [section], Gaṇanātha; in the second, Sadāśiva;
in the third, the goddess Sundarī; in the fourth, the Supreme Deity;
and in the fifth, all the gods—thus did the most excellent teacher, Sarvajit, [arrange them].
Having uttered the benediction, he should then perform the formal declaration (saṅkalpa) according to the prescribed rules.
One should place pearls, rubies, lapis lazuli, hessonite, diamonds, corals,
sapphires, emeralds, and rubies into five jars;
then the true guru himself should personally recite the root mantra one thousand times.
Then, having performed the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa), one should thereafter perform the ritual placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa).
One should adorn the disciple with flowers and other ornaments and smear him with sandalwood paste;
then, having sprinkled the disciple with waters contained in jars made of jewels and other materials.
Then, placing his hand upon the head of the disciple, the best of gurus should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times while uttering the root mantra on the disciple's cheek.
Then [one should recite] the seer, the meter, the peg (kīlaka), and thereafter the seed-syllable of Śakti;
then, at one time, one should mutter the Gāyatrī three times into the right ear.
Then the mantra should be proclaimed; the initiation for women is performed once from the left.
This is the rule for the twice-born, while for women and śūdras it is from the left.
Then, O Goddess, one should prostrate before the Śrī Guru who possesses all auspicious marks;
having personally recited the mantra, one should then perform the rites beginning with the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
This initiation is proclaimed for all the Tārā mantras;
the worship of the earthen Śiva must be performed, and not otherwise.
The general *arghya* offering should be prepared, as well as the specific [offerings] beginning with the seat (*āsana*).
From the base of the womb (*yoni*) to the Viṣṇu-seat (*viṣṇupīṭha*), and from the tip of the *liṅga* to its base—
this constitutes the drawing of the three lines (*trisūtrīkaraṇa*) down to the end of the remaining portion below the womb.
O Sovereign of the Gods! he who does not worship the Śivaliṅga should not worship a king.
He obtains no fruit from other forms of worship; instead, the state of being a caṇḍāla arises for him.
Then, having performed meditation upon the deity, one should cause a flower to be placed upon the head;
this is done through the recitation of the Praṇava and the Pāśa mantra for a number of times equal to the Kalās.
Having purified the entire body, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Placing the right hand upon one's own navel and the left hand [therein],
one performs the weighing of the individual soul (jīva) together with the twenty-four principles (tattvas).
Having clearly distinguished the all-pervading Lord, who is composed of all splendor and has the form of a lamp-flame,
one should unite the entire wheel within the Supreme Brahman.
One should burn the entire body with the flame of the fire at the *mūlādhāra*,
including the whole form of the body, along with its sins and its personhood.
Holding the right nostril, one who performs the recitation for a number of *kalās*,
and having then filled the breath with sixty-four recitations;
One should retain the supreme vital air (vāyu) and then recite [the mantra] thirty-two times.
One should exhale the breath through the left nostril and destroy the subtle body (liṅgadeha).
O Goddess, one should recite the seed-syllable of fire according to the previously mentioned number;
then, having meditated upon everything as consisting of ashes, there follows the ejection of the ashes.
Then, having recited the seed-syllable of the Earth (laṃ), one should inundate the body with that [syllable];
thus filled with the knowledge that "Mahāviṣṇu is himself manifest," one should proceed.
Furthermore, having stabilized one's own body by means of the lunar seed-syllable (*candrabīja*) and sixty-four recitations, one should perform the retention (*kumbhaka*) of the circle of air.
One should purge with the nectar resulting from thirty-two recitations of the Vāruṇa mantra;
then, through supreme devotion, one should accomplish the charming, divine form.
Having visualized the moon upon his forehead, he should apply sacred ash;
then, taking milk and dry ashes into his left hand.
One should cause the mixture of the sacrificial ashes to be applied to the ashes of a bull.
There, one should mutter the six-syllabled mantra of Śiva;
O Dear One, having muttered the five-syllabled mantra sixteen times,
O Great Goddess, one should then recite these two mantras again there.
Oṃ, fire is ashes; water is ashes; the supreme destroyer of all is ashes.
One should place the eyes and the senses within the ashes for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the individual soul through the grace of Śambhu.
Oṃ. The supreme Brahman is said to be the form of ash, and the supreme Śakti is likewise described as such.
Ash should be known as the supreme knowledge, the very nature of the supreme reality.
I wear that sacred ash, which bestows supreme bliss and is established in the ritual manual of knowledge,
for the sake of liberation from the bonds of Paśu.
Thereafter, the Śūdra, having recited the prose-mantra for Brahmā— which consists of six syllables—
and the five-syllable mantra, should always maintain them.
Having assumed the deer-mudrā, one should place it auspiciously upon the forehead;
then, with the root mantra or even with the *praṇava*, one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
The holding of the nostrils with the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb—
this is to be known as *prāṇāyāma*, consisting of inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*).
One should expel four *kalās* of that [breath] with double the force;
having performed this three times in successive order, one should worship even with the mind.
Even for the wise, success shall come if they perform this nyāsa:
"Salutation to Paśupati on the head; salutation to Hari on the mouth."
One should place [the mantra] for Śrī Nīlakaṇṭha Rudra on the throat, and for Dhūmranetra on the chest; at the root, one should offer salutations to Śrī Śambhu.
To Bhairava at the two feet, to Śiva on the right arm,
to Kalā on the left arm, and likewise to Jñāna on the back.
One should assign Krodha to all the limbs during the worship of Śiva;
then, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅgaka*) with the seed-syllable (*bīja*) possessing the six long vowels.
Having likewise performed the placement of the limbs and hands, one should carry out the binding of the ten directions.
Having uttered "Salutation to Hara," one who is pure should fetch the clay.
One should perform the invocation with the name of Maheśvara ending in the dative case and followed by "namaḥ";
having uttered "O Trident-bearer," one should say, "Be well-established here yourself."
Then, having performed the installation and offered [the oblation] once it is accomplished, one should invoke and worship [the deity].
Having offered water for the feet, the arghya, fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp,
and food offerings and the like, one should worship the Supreme Lord.
O Great Goddess, I accept the worship of that self-restrained person who offers a plantain fruit along with its stalk to the Śiva-liṅga.
O Goddess! His accomplishment shall always be certain and fruitful.
Standing before it, the wise one should mutter the root mantra ten thousand times; he should then install the linga with the formula: "Obeisance to Paśupati."
Indeed, who is truly capable of describing the greatness of the bilva leaf?
O Goddess, worship of the Liṅga without bilva leaves is indeed fruitless.
One should worship the eightfold form of Śiva with supreme devotion;
having worshipped them ending in the southeast, one should then sacrifice to Śiva upon the altar and in the liṅga.
The pedestal of the *liṅga* is the Goddess, and the *liṅga* itself is Maheśvara manifest;
by worshipping those two, both the Goddess and the God become well-worshipped.
Oṃ, homage to Sarva, whose form is the earth; Oṃ, homage to Bhava, whose form is water;
homage to Rudra, whose form is fire; Oṃ, homage to Ugra, whose form is wind; [homage] to Bhīma.

Salutation to the one whose form is space; Oṃ, salutation to Paśupati, whose form is the sacrificer; Oṃ, salutation to Mahādeva, whose form is the moon; Oṃ, salutation to Īśāna, whose form is the sun.
With this, one should worship the eight forms.
O Goddess! One should offer three handfuls of flowers to Śaṅkara;
he obtains the fruit of worship, not otherwise than from worshipping a hundred thousand times.
Then, O Goddess, one should perform the root-mantra recitation one hundred and eight times;
while reciting it, one should offer bilva leaves with water to the Liṅga.
Oṃ! You are the protector of the most secret of secrets; accept this recitation performed by us.
May success be mine, O God! By your grace, O Maheśvara!
Regarding the phrase "O Maheśvara," some manuscripts read "sthitvā tvayi" (having stood in you).
The hymn (*stotra*) and the armor (*kavaca*) should be sought in works such as the *Liṅgārcanacandrikā*. Thereafter, one should perform the playing of musical instruments and other rites.
He who, having worshipped the earthen linga,
performs vocal music or likewise produces the sound of clapping with the palms of his hands, attains union with Śiva.
Having performed half a circumambulation, one should bow to the Lord of Pārvatī;
then one should go from the southern side to the northern side, and there again perform the return movement.
Placing the hands on the back and likewise the two knees on the ground,
and bowing the head, one assumes the shape of a half-moon.
O Maheśvarī! Whoever should give a vessel for the sacred knowledge to Śaṅkara, the merit of performing a horse sacrifice is produced by that single vessel.
O Goddess, on the twelfth day, having beheld the earthen *liṅga* of Śaṅkara,
one should take a vessel of *sambidā* and offer everything with palms joined in reverence.
That man who never worships even the *liṅga* of Śaṅkara—
whether he be a devotee of Viṣṇu, a Śākta, or a Śaiva— is the lowest of men.
Having gratified Śiva by the recitation of the names of dance, song, and instrumental music, one should dismiss him with the *saṃhāramudrā*,
saying "Forgive me," and then consecrate the site.
O Goddess, if a man, having worshipped the earthen linga of Hara,
should place it in water, he will certainly become poor.
Having worshipped the supreme Liṅga dear to Pārvatī,
he who installs it on the earth during the Raudra period goes to Dandaśūka.
Having worshipped the Śivaliṅga, one should indeed consign it to the earth;
or else, if one installs it in water, that man goes to Dandaśūka.

Wherever there is mention of hell, the wise should not perform [the rite]; nor should one perform it for those who are impoverished. However, since both faults are heard in the *Mahāliṅgeśvaratantra*, and because of the scriptural statement, "The man shall go to the world of biting serpents," one should simply place [the remains] upon the ground.
In the absence of that [water], one should cast it into water. One should not worship Śambhu in water other than the waters of the Bhāgīrathī;
nor should one worship Śambhu in water other than the waters of the Bhāgīrathī. Thus it is stated in the Yāmala.

This has been explained by my guru, Tripurānanda. Regarding worship, [one should not perform it] even with *vilva* leaves and so forth in ordinary water, let alone in the waters of the Gaṅgā. The meaning is that one should not place [the deity] in ordinary water, nor should one worship through the display of mudrās and the like. Thus, it is stated in the Tārānigama:
And in the Mahāliṅgeśvara Tantra:
"He who, residing within the three worlds, should worship Kālī, Tārā, or Sundarī without first worshipping the earthen [liṅga], shall go to the torments of Yama."
Regarding the statement that one should first worship Mahāvidyā and then perform the worship of Śiva, that is not found in the *Liṅgārcanacandrikā*. [It states:
"Having worshipped Mahāvidyā, one should perform the worship of Śiva."
O Goddess! By performing it otherwise, one shall not obtain the fruit of the worship.
Thus ends the speech of Śiva for the purpose of praising the Mahāvidyās. Likewise, it is stated in the Tripurākalpa:
"As long as the lowest of practitioners does not worship the earthen liṅga..."
Sundarī, Tārakā, and Asitā do not accept his worship.
Thus ends the chapter on the worship of the Śivaliṅga in the second chapter of the *Tārārahasya*, composed by the wandering ascetic teacher Tīrthāvadhūta, a Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka of Brahmananda.
In the *Śaktisāra*:
First, one should perform the morning duties; after that, the morning twilight ritual (saṃdhyā);
then, having performed the bath, likewise the midday twilight ritual.
Then one should perform the worship of Śiva, as well as the internal sacrifice (antaryajana), O Śiva!
Thereafter, the formal worship should be performed, and then one should carry out the fire-oblation (homa).
Then one should offer the bali-oblation, and after that, perform the fire-sacrifice (homa);
having offered enjoyments to Mahādevī, one should perform the evening twilight ritual (sāyaṃsandhyā).
Then yoga should be practiced, and thereafter the supreme means of accomplishment;
having attained such a state, one should practice the Tāraka [mantra] if one so desires.
Then one attains perfection; not otherwise, even in ten million eons.
Then, for the sake of accomplishing his purpose, the best of practitioners should recite the hymn and the armor-mantra known as the *Sahasranāma* at the three junctions of the day.
By this, the necessity of performing internal worship (*antaryajana*) within the Śiva-pūjā is established; that very point is written here. In the *Tārāsāra* and the *Nigama*:
"O Śiva! One does not obtain the fruit of worship without internal worship."
Therefore, prior to the external worship, one should perform the internal sacrifice.
And likewise, in the Ekajaṭā-pakṣa:
"One should meditate upon the supreme ocean of nectar within one's own heart,
and in its center, an island of jewels consisting of golden sand."
There is the Pārijāta grove and also the temple of jewels;
having visualized the cremation ground there, one should meditate upon the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma) therein.
In its center is a jeweled pedestal adorned with various gems,
decorated in the four directions with corpses, skulls, funeral pyres, charcoal, and bones.
Having meditated with effort, the practitioner of mantra should himself dwell on the island of reality;
he should always contemplate Mahādeva, the teacher of the world, in the aperture of Brahmā.
Having visualized the goddess Tārā, whose form is that of the Savior (Tāra), seated to his left, one should prostrate to the Vidyā; this is declared to be the morning ritual.
At the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), there is the supreme sacred ford (tīrtha) in the form of a drop (bindu);
there the practitioner should perform a bath that removes all impurities.
And having placed Śivatīrtha in the heart in the form of the seed-syllable *badhū*,
the best of practitioners should bathe within the central *suṣumnā* channel.
Thus is the ritual bath.
With one-pointed mind, one should meditate upon a lion-throne within one's own heart;
there, a couch consisting of the nature of knowledge and bliss is envisioned.
Then, one should visualize Śiva there, adorned with all ornaments,
naked, of massive body, and intoxicated by the state of passion.
The foremost of practitioners should visualize his own phallus erect upon the bed;
thereafter, he should visualize the Goddess, whose nature is the bliss of nectar.
One should contemplate the Goddess’s braid of hair, which possesses the luster of molten gold, is adorned with various ornaments, and is entwined with *pārijāta* flowers.
The twilight ritual (saṃdhyā) should be performed at the three junctions of the day by one who desires the accomplishment of mantra.
The Goddess Kāmeśvarī is the mother, and Śiva Kāmeśvara is the father;
by being faithful and meditating upon them, one shall become a master of the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭasiddhi).
Thus ends the twilight meditation (*sandhyā*).
[One should meditate upon] the Goddess, who consists of all splendor, the power of Śiva, whose nature is self-restraint,
who possesses the luster of the blazing sun, fire, and moon, and whose radiance is equal to ten million flashes of lightning.
"The practitioner who is unwavering through the yoga of meditation should perform meditative cultivation.
Thus, meditation should be practiced by practitioners for the sake of attaining mantra-siddhi. This concludes the section on meditation.
One should satisfy the Supreme Tāriṇī from the moon-vessel at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra);
and from the sun-vessel situated there, one should offer a beautiful arghya.
Compassion, knowledge, forbearance, merit, and restraint of the senses are flowers;
the gift of knowledge is a meritorious flower, and non-violence is the supreme flower.
O Goddess! You should give me the flower of conduct, the supreme self-arisen flower, the flower of bliss, and the flower for the worship of the practitioner.
He who offers ten flowers shall go to the station of Tāraka;
that best of practitioners should worship with auspicious substances found throughout the three worlds.
One should offer the *tattva* (the ritual substance) together with fish and meat to the Tārakā;
then one attains perfection, not through recitation nor through the worship of the *kula*. Thus ends the worship.
The Lord of the *Kula* should perform recitation with the garlands of syllables preceded by the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
One should place the sixteen-spoked [mandala] within the heart-lotus and assign the sixteen vowels.
Beginning from the east and proceeding to the leaf in the southeast corner,
the wise one should place the four letters beginning with *ka* upon the *ādhāra*.
Having assigned [the mantras] starting from the western petal and ending with the northern one,
the excellent practitioner should assign them at the base of the liṅga upon the six-petaled lotus in the sequence beginning from the north.

The best of practitioners should place the six syllables beginning with *ṅa* and ending with *ña* at the root of the navel; he should then place the charming syllables beginning with *ṭa* and ending with *ḍha*.
Having assigned the great mantras in the form of syllables according to the sequence starting from the south,
one should place them at the root of the palate upon the fourteen-petaled lotus.
The wise one should place the letters beginning with *dha* and ending with *sa*, which have the color of Indra, [on the face];
and he should always place the two letters *ha* and *kṣa* between the eyebrows on the forehead.

First, for the sake of perfect accomplishment, the wise practitioner should certainly place the twelve syllables beginning with 'ka' and ending with 'ṭha' upon the white petals on the right and likewise on the left.
One should always place the letters beginning with *ḍa* and ending with the *visarga* upon the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra*).
O Pārvatī, in this way, there is no need for the placement (*nyāsa*) of the internal *mātṛkās*.
But he who performs internal worship shall go to the abode of Yama.
Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) ending with the *mātṛkā*, one should recite [the mantra] with the garland of letters (*varṇamālā*).
That [garland] consists of the letters from *a* to *kṣa*, with the letters *ha* and *kṣa* in the middle;
joined with the *nāda* and *bindu*, one should recite the mantra at the end of the letters.
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times in both forward and reverse order;
one should perform the recitation according to the eight groups of consonants: u, ku, cu, ṭu, tu, pu, yu, and śu.

U is the class of vowels (svaravarga), consisting of sixteen sounds. Ku is the ka-class (kavarga), cu is the ca-class (cavarga), ṭu is the ṭa-class (ṭavarga), tu is the ta-class (tavarga), pu is the pa-class (pavarga), and yu is the ya-class (yavarga), which consists of four sounds. Śu is the śa-class (śavarga), which consists of six sounds; thus it is stated in the Tārārṇava.
Endowed with both *nāda* and *bindu*, it is established within all phonemes;
for women and *śūdras*, this very [mantra] is devoid of *nāda* and *bindu*.
When conjoined with *nāda* and *bindu*, it bestows liberation during recitation and ritual placement (*nyāsa*).

By this, because liberation is heard [promised] for all castes, there is eligibility for the recitation (*japa*) and ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the syllables adorned with half-moons and crescents. However, for women and Śūdras, there is no application of the visarga, *ukāra*, or *bindu* along with the crescent moon. And so it is said:
In the *Tārāsāra*, the wielder of the trident states: "One should not practice recitation or ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with a syllable that lacks the moon;
otherwise, by acting in this way, the fool certainly goes to hell."
One should meditate within one's own heart upon the supreme yoni-maṇḍala,
which is triangular, possesses all colors, and is surrounded by kings.
Having meditated upon the womb of Kāmākhyā while recollecting the blue lotus,
one should mentally offer oblations sixteen times with clarified butter produced from the liṅga.

Then one should perform three circumambulations of Śivā mentally; such is the internal worship. If a fool performs the worship of the Supreme Tārā without having performed this, he does not obtain the fruit of the worship for ten million lifetimes.
Thus ends the internal sacrifice.
Now follows the internal sacrifice of Ugratārā.
Now I shall describe the inner sacrifice (antaryāga) of Ugratārā:
one should meditate upon the supreme ocean of nectar within one's own heart.
In the sixteen-petaled heart-lotus, one should satisfy Ugratāriṇī,
recollecting the root mantra for each and every petal of the great goddess.
O child! One should now offer oblations into her womb with this mantra:
"Oṃ! Into the fire whose nature is the consciousness of the navel, I offer the oblation with the mind as the sacrificial ladle."
With the ladle of *unmanī*, grasped by the two hands of light and space, I perpetually offer the sensory functions into the path of the *suṣumṇā*.
I offer [myself] as an oblation into the fire filled with the oil of the subtle portions of dharma and adharma.
Then, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times using the rosary of letters;
having performed circumambulation and prostrated, one may proceed at ease.
Thus ends the internal worship of Ugratārā.
One should meditate within one's own heart upon Sāradā in her blue form—
the Goddess standing in the pratyālīḍha posture, with a tiger skin wrapped around her waist.
One should worship Nīlasarasvatī, who has a smiling face, is most formidable,
is intent on inverted sexual union, and bestows the status of Lord of Speech.
Having caused [the disciple] to drink a stream of nectar accompanied by fish and meat,
one should place the liquor mixed with meat into the mouth with a small spoon.
In the great heart, one should meditate upon the supreme Mistress of the Gods, who possesses a blue voice and whose heart is intoxicated by the nectar [of Śiva],
again and again in the mouth of Śiva.
O Great Goddess! Holding her lotus-foot with his own hand, he indeed kisses it as it falls through the force of the wind.
Having risen, he should kiss the face of the Tāriṇī again and again;
and he should place a fish and great liquor that has been burnt upon his mouth.
Burnt fish, burnt meat, blood from the body of a sacrificial animal,
the flesh of a boar’s snout, and likewise the nectar of the vulva and the phallus.
One should offer the remnants to Nīlasarasvatī at the mouth of Hara;
having worshipped again and again, one should worship with a rosary of letters.
Thus has been described the most beautiful internal worship of Nīlavāṇī.
O Great Goddess! He who worships with supreme devotion—within his hand shall always dwell [the deity]; all perfections shall abide there, and speech shall certainly dwell within his mouth.
For one who thus contemplates day and night within the Kula tradition,
both worldly enjoyment and liberation, as well as the fulfillment of all desires, shall reside in the palm of his hand.
