Thus ends the internal worship of Nīlasarasvatī.
Now follows the extraction of the mantra of Ekajaṭā:
for those of castes other than Brāhmaṇas, a hexagon situated upon the pericarp [is required].
For Brahmins, the triangle should always be drawn situated within the pericarp.
In the center, the wise one should draw the *kūrca* syllable, and after that, two circles;
then an eight-petaled lotus should be drawn, endowed with four seed-syllables.
In the east, *la* and *jā* are the bride; in the south, *va*; in the north, *pha* is proclaimed;
in the west, *ṭaṃ* is declared; and in the corner, it is joined with *reṇukā*.
One should draw a very beautiful yantra that is square and has four doors.
Thus, having abandoned the [original] yantra, one should worship it in a different yantra;
having given a curse to her in anger, the Goddess departs toward Hara.
Immediately after that, I shall describe the differentiation of this Tārā;
one should draw a triangle, three circles, and also a four-petaled lotus.
Then, for the worship of Kāmatārā, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus, followed by two circles, and then a square with four gates.
The yantra for their retention is as follows: one should draw a triangle called the "name of the practitioner," followed by a hexagon,
and then an eight-petaled lotus joined with the sixteen vowels.
"And one should encircle [the site] with the seven-syllable mantra of Padmāvatī;
it should be square, with four gates, and equipped with vajras in the corners. Thus it is said.
Now, the Yantra of Ugratārā:
First, one should draw a nine-cornered figure provided with five petals;
it should have two circles and a double-layered lotus, all adorned with pollen-dust.
For the worship of Ugratārā, [the mandala] is square with four gates,
hexagonal and quadrangular, and provided with five circles.
One should draw an eight-petalled lotus, as well as a square and so forth;
then a circle joined with a point (bindu), and after that a hexagon;
one should then draw an eight-petalled lotus and, after that, the earth-house (bhūgṛha).
Now, the Yantra of Nīlatāriṇī:
One should draw three equal triangles, with a point (bindu) in the center;
know that there are two circles, a six-petalled lotus, and a twelve-petalled lotus within three circles.
Furthermore, three circles should be drawn, forming a house consisting of four doors;
likewise, a double triangle, a hexagon, a circle, and an eight-petaled lotus.
Furthermore, the house consists of four doors with petals shaped like crescent moons;
this common mechanism is applicable everywhere as stated in the section on Ekajaṭā. Thus concludes the extraction of the human yantra.
Now, the consecration of the yantra: In the Tārānigama it is said:
"In a copper vessel, or in a skull, or in one made of wood from a cremation ground..."
One should construct the yantra according to the prescribed rules using gold, silver, or iron.
Regarding the permanence of the *saṃskāra*, it is said in the *Tārāsāra*:
"But those lowest of men who worship in an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) yantra—
being devoid of merit, knowledge, and a son— how can there be accomplishments (*siddhi*) in their practice?"
If those who have drawn the yantra do not perform worship day after day, the gods will not accept their worship; how then can there be spiritual attainment?
In that very same [text]: "One who is unable to draw the diagram (*yantra*) should worship in a flower-diagram,
or in *aparā*, *javā*, *droṇa*, or *karavīraka*."
One should worship on a slab of Gauri, or even on the vessel of the principles (tattva-pātra) of Śiva; in the absence of all these yantras, one should worship upon a śālagrāma stone or in water.
One should worship all the castes along with their wives in that yantra;
however, in a yantra other than the Śālagrāma, the worship of Śūdra women is recommended.
In the worship of Gaurī, however, [the image] should be made of stone and so forth, but not of clay.

Likewise, in the Śaktiyāmala: "If, during worship on an earthen altar (pārthiva-yoni-vedi), one fails to use dust [as a purifier], one is cooked in a terrible hell; there is no liberation for ten million births. Thus it is said.
Seated upon a red seat, the hero, facing the direction of Kāmākhyā,
should draw an eight-petalled lotus with saffron for the sake of perfect accomplishment.
Therein one should establish the yantra and sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
one should gaze upon it with the root mantra and strike it with flowers using the weapon mantra (astra).
One should deposit the drops with the root mantra and smear [the area] with sandalwood paste;
having worshipped the yantra with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains, one should gaze upon it.
Oṃ, we know the King of Yantras; we meditate upon the Support of All; may that Yantra inspire us.
With this Gāyatrī as well, one should consecrate it with hundreds of recitations.
Having attained the state of the deity, one should recite the root mantra a hundred times;
having also performed the consecration according to the sequence prescribed for installation, one should gaze upon it.
One should consecrate that [object] one hundred times with the Gāyatrī mantra;
having invoked the Goddess there, one should consecrate it with the Daśamūla [mantra].
Having offered eight handfuls of flowers, one should worship with the ritual services (upacāras),
using either ten or five ancillary rites (kalās) according to one's capacity.
Then, having performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*), one should offer oblations (*homa*) one hundred and eight times;
if one is unable to perform the rite of *homa*, one should perform double the number of recitations (*japa*).
Having prostrated, one should always wear that yantra for the attainment of true being;
it should be caused to be made by a guru, or one should purify it oneself.
O Harasundarī! Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and even women of the Śūdra caste have the right to participate in this virtuous rite.
In every instance of fire-offering, worship, or the consecration of a child,
as well as in ritual application where one is thoroughly purified, [this applies] during the rite of consecrating a garland.
In the practice involving corpses, funeral pyres, and creepers, the syllable *lajjā* (the "shame" mantra) occupies the place of the *praṇava*; the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* is the beloved of Fire.
Know that at the site of Setu is the Kūrca-bīja, and in the Ṣoḍhā-nyāsa is the Kāma-bīja; these bestow heaven and liberation everywhere, even for Śūdra women.

Thus ends the second chapter, on the consecration of the yantra, in the *Tārārahasya* composed by the venerable Brahmānanda, the wandering mendicant and ascetic of the Paramahaṃsa order. Now begins the section on the rosary (*mālā*). In the *Tārānigama*:
A rosary fashioned from a fragment of a human skull,
or a garland made of great conch shells, is traditionally held to bestow spiritual accomplishments (siddhi) spontaneously.
It may be fashioned from ivory or likewise from the joints of the fingers;
therein the Great Vidyā Kālī Tārā remains unwearied.
O Śaṅkara, in the absence [of a rosary], one may use a crystal rosary or a great conch shell;
having purified it, one should recite the mantra for the accomplishment of all desires and aims.
O child! By reciting [the mantra] on a great conch shell, one shall suddenly become a possessor of siddhis;
through a crystal [rosary], there is success in mantra; and with rudrākṣa, one becomes a possessor of all siddhis.
In rites for peace, there should be a knot of kuśa grass; in killing, one made of bamboo;
in expulsion, one of horse-teeth; and in subjugation, a garland of coral.
For the attainment of knowledge, wealth, and women,
as well as for the attraction [of others] and the paralyzing of enemies, a rosary made of silver is likewise [recommended].
He speaks of the permanence regarding the ritual action: "The goddess, having angrily cast a curse upon that man who mutters the mantra with unrefined garlands, goes toward Hara."
One should draw a triangle on the ground and place the rosary there.
With the mantra for the installation of the deity, one should install the Goddess therein. Having consecrated the *tattva* with that same [mantra], one should scatter a thousand dots.
One should worship the supreme Tāriṇī with sindūra, karavīra, and other offerings,
as well as with a garland untouched by tulasī or cow dung, and touched by the Gaṅgā.
One should guard it with great effort and not show it even to one's guru.
O Goddess of Gods, even for the bone of one who has met an untimely death or of one other than a Brahmin,
one should diligently take that bone and thread it into a garland using a tube (dhamanī) or else with a red thread during the piercing of a woman's ear.
Thus ends the Great Conch Garland. Now, the general garland:
for killing, fifteen; for uprooting, eighteen.
Likewise, with twenty-eight garlands, one should perform subjugation as well as attraction.
For the sake of wealth, one should perform thirty recitations; for success, twenty-five;
and with fifty-one mantras, one shall attain all perfections.
If there is a Brahmin girl who remains unmarried in her body,
one should fashion for her a garland made of sacred threads that brings all happiness.
For pacification, there should be a cotton thread; for accomplishment, a red thread;
for the form of knowledge, a colored thread; and for killing, a black thread.
For attraction, a blue thread is used; the vein grants all accomplishments.
Having tripled it three times, it is provided with a firm cord.
One should make a knot by wrapping [the thread] two and a half times so that it is firm;
one may also make a knot provided with a *brahmagranthi* or wrapped three times.
Alternatively, one may place a knotted bead there along with a strong cord;
this rosary, consisting of merit, is considered to bestow all spiritual accomplishments.
Now, the purification:
One should fashion a semi-circular shape using nine leaves of the *aśvattha* tree;
in its center, one should place the rosary while reciting the root mantra of the *mātṛkā*.
One should wash it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and rub it with the Vāmadeva mantra.
Vāmadeva, however, states in the *Mahākulārṇava*: "Oṃ, to Vāmadeva, the lord of all siddhis, the remover of all sins, the lord of all garlands—oṃ huṃ oṃ aiṃ klūṃ phaṭ.
With this [mantra], one should rub [the substance] with sandalwood, saffron, gorocanā, and so forth.
Vāmadeva, who is Vedic, must not be led astray by those ignorant of reality;
for the Vedas do not yield fruit for those devoid of the Kula practice.

"Oṃ, Lajjā, Subhagā, Vāgbhavā, and Kāma—by means of these, one should perform the gazing for the successful accomplishment of the Tārā mantra. Thus one should gaze. Then, one should perform [the consecration] with the root mantra recited one hundred times. Then, with the letters of the Mātṛkā...
One should drop each individual drop upon the images and satisfy the Goddess with the root mantra.
One should bathe the rosary with the root mantra and also smear it with saffron.
One should rub it according to the rules with clarified butter and worship it with the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja).
Then, one should indeed recite the root mantra a hundred times over the rosary;
there, one should install the Goddess according to the prescribed rite of installation.

Then, one should perform the invocation with the *āvāhana-mudrās*. Thereafter, one should worship with either the sixteen or the five services (*upacāras*). Then, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations (*homa*). If that is impossible, there should be double the number of recitations (*japa*). Then, having performed seven circumambulations and having practiced breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), [one should proceed].
Having performed the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) on the hands and body, one should place the rosary upon the head and conceal it.
One should join mouth to mouth and attach tail to tail;
the practitioner of mantra should recite from the mouth, never from the tail.
If one recites [the mantra] for someone who asks about sorrow, suffering, fear, and so forth,
it is said that even for such a person, the goddess consigns them to hell with palms joined in reverence.
There will be no good rebirth nor any accomplishment; obstacles shall always arise for him.
When the sound occurs, disease ensues, and shaking [the head] brings much suffering. From contempt, there is loss of accomplishment; therefore, one should be diligent.
Thus concludes the consecration of the rosary.
Now follows the fire oblation (*homa*).
One should draw three lines, one with its tip pointing eastward and two with their tips pointing northward.
And in the middle of that, one should apply a plaster in four squares according to the prescribed rule.
First, one should draw a triangle; then, in its center, one with the *lajjā* (the seed-syllable of the Goddess);
then a circle, and then a hexagon with four vajras at its corners.
At the outer corner of the door is an elephant’s frontal globe; at the two doors are two yonis each.
The wheel is endowed with eight yonis, and there are four elephant’s frontal globes.
Having thus prepared either a sacrificial pit or a leveled altar, one should meditate upon the Goddess;
one should worship Viṣṇu in the fire and the Wielder of the Trident (Śiva) in the northeast.
One should worship Brahmā in the northwest and Indra in the southwest;
one should worship Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī in the two eastern triangles.
One should worship Śacī and Kṛṣṇā in the north, Chāyā and Gaṅgā in the west,
and the goddess Durgā and Tripuṭā in the south.
One should worship Mukunda, Īśa, and Purandara at the tips of the eastern [blades];
and one should indeed worship Brahmā, Vaivasvata, and Indu at the tips of the northern [blades].
O Sadāśiva, one should thereafter worship the Goddess within the six corners:
Durgā, Kāñcī, Kālī, Tripurā, and Bhairavī.
One should worship Asitā in the corner, the deliverer Tāriṇī who bestows liberation;
O child, one should worship her in the center with offerings according to one's capacity.
Then, having visualized the womb of the Goddess, one should contemplate it as being filled with *rajas*.
Having offered three handfuls of flowers, one should cast the wood into it.
Then, having brought the auspicious fire situated in a bronze vessel, the wise one should offer [the oblation] with this mantra: "Oṃ kravyādebhyo huṃ phaṭ svāhā."
Having brought it back again by means of the root mantra, one should place it within the center of the *yoni*.
Then, having displayed the *yonimudrā*, one should recite the root mantra there ten times.
There, having meditated upon the Goddess, one should worship the Goddess Sarvārthasādhinī with fragrant flowers and with menstrual blood (rajas) upon the circle of the womb (yoni-maṇḍala).
Oṃ cit piṅgala! Strike, strike! Cook, cook! Grind, grind! Destroy, destroy!
Devour, devour my wicked, sinful beings and enemies! Drink, drink!
By means of this fire offering, make all ignorance known [to them] and accomplish all my tasks, svāhā!
Having recited this, one should blow upon the fire:
"Arisen from the quality of passion (rajas), red in color, three-eyed, two-armed, the destroyer of all sins, fully kindled, and facing in all directions."
Adorned with various ornaments and endowed with many tongues.

Having meditated thus, one should assign the name by saying, "O Fire, you are named Varada (the Giver of Boons)," and then invoke him with: "O Fire named Varada, come here, stay here, stay; accomplish all my rites, svāhā! Then one should pay obeisance with the root mantra. The same applies to the clarified butter (ājya).

And regarding the *śruva* ladle: having taken clarified butter from the southern part of the *ājya* vessel, one should offer it into the right eye of the fire with the root mantra (*mūla*). Likewise, having taken clarified butter from the left part, [one offers it] into the left eye;
and from the middle, into the middle eye. Then, with the *mahāvyāhṛtis*: *oṃ bhūḥ svāhā*.
*Oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā*. *Oṃ svaḥ svāhā*. *Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥsvaḥ svāhā*.

[These are] except for women and Śūdras. Then, having offered eleven oblations with the root mantra, [one offers]: *To the deities of the seat (pīṭha) of the venerable goddess Tārā, svāhā*. Then, [an oblation] to Akṣobhya, the seer (*ṛṣi*). Then, if it is for a rite of desire (*kāmyakarma*)...

If it was not intended to be permanent, then after completing the prescribed oblation with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), one who is neither a woman nor a *śūdra* should offer oblations with the *mahāvyāhṛtis*,
and then offer eight oblations to the deities of the enclosure.

Having worshipped the fire with perfumes, flowers, garlands, and betel, and having offered three oblations with the *śruva* ladle to Śrī Sadāśiva using the root mantra, one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the fire with the root mantra.

Having circumambulated [the deity] and prostrated, and having offered the desired sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth, one should apply the *tilaka* with the root mantra using the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, and then dismiss [the deity] with the words "Forgive me" (*kṣamasva*). Thus ends the fire sacrifice (*homa*).

In this auspicious *Tārārahasya*, a work on the excellent means for the realization of Brahman-bliss, where Kamalā sits with palms joined in reverence and Sāradā holds her lute, [the author] recollects the words of Tārā regarding her beloved, who is the cause of her leftward speech.
The second chapter, beginning with initiation, bestows accomplishment swiftly.
Now begins the third chapter:
the expiation for the forgetting of mantras. This is according to the *Tārānigama* and the *Tārārṇava*; the regulations for other [mantras] are found elsewhere.
If there should be confusion regarding the mantra in the Kālī or Tārā Vidyās,
one should then perform the worship of Tārā at a solitary liṅga in a temple of Śiva.
Seated upon a kusha-grass mat, the hero should recite the Padmāvatī mantra eleven thousand times; thereafter, the recollection of the mantra will arise.
In the mantras of Kālī and Tārā, there is no concern regarding the maṇḍala;
the world is never defiled by the faults of enemies, defects, or other such evils.
O Goddess, if by the power of fortune the Tārā mantra is obtained,
one need not examine there the wheels of debtors, creditors, and so forth.
In the midst of the Tārā-vidyā-cakra, one shall never be wealthy;
but having attained the Mahācīna-krama, one becomes a debtor to all.
Therefore, even at the cost of his life, the practitioner should not abandon the Mahācīna [practice] during the sadhana or the worship of the goddess Tārā.
The man who does not accomplish the Mahācīna and Mahānīla [mantras] has no power in their accomplishment; he is tormented in the Kumbhīpāka hell.
Having abandoned the left-hand practice (vāmācāra), if one performs worship or recitation,
he shall go to a terrible hell for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
O Goddess! Without the practice of the left-hand path (vāmācāra), the worship of Tārā leads to sorrow and death in this world, and to hell in the next.
He who has no worship, no recitation, no twilight ritual, and no libation,
yet performs the Mahācīnakrama, shall go to the state of the Savior.
O Goddess! Without the five principles (pañcatattva), even a Brāhmaṇa falls to the state of a Śūdra; O Goddess! Endowed with the five principles, even a Śūdra attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Shudras, and even those born of the lowest castes—
by performing the Mahachinakrama, Shiva himself becomes manifest.
When a Kaula sees another Kaula and does not perform worship for him,
or while remaining in the *cakra*, the practitioner of mantra (*mantrī*) should practice the *latāyoga*.
The Kaula, situated in the central wheel, does not set his mind upon giving [the essence] to the Śaktis or to the practitioner; rather, he proceeds to take it up himself.
Alternatively, having reached the day [of the festival], one should not perform the family worship;
nor should one satisfy the practitioners and the Śaktis with acts of unrestrained conduct.
Or, with a serene mind, it is offered to a true Kaula;
and the Kula-rite is performed by oneself together with one's own kinsmen.
His yantra, his rosary, his very manual of worship,
and the armor worn by him are snatched away by the hosts of Yoginīs.
It may be consumed by fire, or dissolved in water;
it may be carried away by thieves, or seized in part by hosts of yoginīs.
If it should happen thus, O dear one, O Śiva!— the seizing of the machine and so forth—
then, having brought together five Kaulas and especially a virgin girl...
Having worshipped with perfumes and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), the excellent practitioner, bowing his head, should pay homage;
he should then perform one thousand *homa* offerings in the center of the wheel.
The best of practitioners should perform one hundred and eight libations even with the liquor of scorched fish; thus, he is not tainted by any defects.
In the event of the destruction of the yantra and other such items, this expiation is prescribed according to the word of Śiva;
it is held that one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times using the garland of letters.
Now follows the consecration of the five principles (*pañcatattvasaṃskāra*).
In a house red with lac, or at the mouth of Kāmākhyā,
the best of practitioners should assume every kind of amorous attire.
Sindūra, saffron, or even kula-candana should be worn;
the Śakti on the left side is adorned with all ornaments.
Having worshipped her with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata),
the practitioner [should draw] a hexagon joined with a dot (bindu), a circle, and also a triangle.
Furthermore, one should draw a four-cornered circle with saffron,
smear it with red sandalwood paste, and encircle it with a red cloth.
Having gazed [upon it] with the root mantra, one should display the yoni-mudrā;
there, one should meditate upon the deity in the form of supreme bliss.
One should prostrate with the five mudrās to the supreme support of the cause;
first with "Hrīṃ Namaḥ" for the yoni-mudrā, and with "Kṣaṃ Namaḥ" while the hands are joined in añjali.
Vluṃ, salutation to the Kula-mudrā; Glauṃ, salutation to the Matsya-rūpaka;
Hauṃ, salutation to the Saṃpuṭa-ākāra; thus the five mudrās have been proclaimed.
One should sprinkle [the object] with the root mantra and fumigate it with that same [mantra].
Then, having offered fragrance and flowers, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Having performed the Nyāsa of the Ṛṣis and so forth, as well as the Nyāsa of the hands, the limbs, and the six limbs, one should then perform the Nyāsa of the syllables and display the five mudrās.
Having placed his hand upon the vessel, he should then recite this unsurpassed mantra over the cow, the vulva, the fish, the conch, and thereafter the sword.
Oṃ! The Supreme Brahman alone is eternal, consisting of both the gross and the subtle;
by that [Brahman], I destroy for you the sin of killing a Brahmin born from a mere thought.
Oṃ! O you who are born from the solar disc! O you who arise from the abode of Varuṇa!
O Goddess, whose essence is the seed-syllable Amā! May [this] be liberated from the curse of Śukra.
Oṃ! If the Praṇava is the seed-syllable of the gods and consists of the bliss of Brahman, by that truth, O Queen of Gods, may it dispel the sin of killing a Brahmin!
Oṃ vāṃ vīṃ vūṃ vaiṃ vauṃ vaḥ, salutations to the Goddess Sudhā, who has been liberated from the curse of Brahmā. Thus one should recite ten times.
The letter *ka* joined with the letter *ra*, combined with the six long vowels, and conjoined with the moon (the nasal bindu).
*Kīṃ krīṃ krūṃ kraiṃ krauṃ kraḥ | Sudhādevyāḥ kṛṣṇaśāpaṃ mocaya mocaya amṛtaṃ śrāvaya śrāvaya svāhā |* Thus one should recite ten times. *Oṃ chāṃ chīṃ chūṃ chaiṃ chauṃ chaḥ churikā bhavaśobhini.*
"Paralyze, paralyze the minds, eyes, and senses of all beasts and people!
Destroy, destroy! Slay, slay!"—thus three times. Oṃ! O Supreme Mistress!
O Carrier of the Void of the Supreme Space! O Consumer of Moon, Sun, and Fire! Enter, enter the vessel!
Svāhā! (Recite this) three times.
In the midst of that, one should contemplate the Goddess, whose form is nectar and bliss, resembling ten million suns in brilliance and as cooling as ten million moons.
"Clad in red garments, adorned with all ornaments,
beautified by jeweled armlets, bracelets, and so forth, possessing every form"— this is the visualization (*dhyāna*).
The practice (*sādhana*) should be performed by excellent practitioners in the midst of nectar.
One should worship her, who delights in the bliss of nectar, with bilva leaves and other offerings.
In the midst of that, one should meditate upon the god Bhairava, beloved of Bhairavī,
situated in the middle of an ocean of nectar, possessing five faces and three eyes.
Mounted upon a bull, blue-throated, adorned with all ornaments,
endowed with eighteen arms, and wielding a mace and a club.
A sword, a shield, a battle-axe, a mallet, a trident, a staff,
a noose, a goad, an arrow, a bow, the mudrā, and a rosary of knowledge.
One should visualize him holding a deer, a skull, and a serpent that assumes all forms, situated in the midst of a mass of matted hair within the center of the nectar.
One should worship Maheśvara, the God of gods, with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.

"Oṃ, may we know Ānandeśvara; may we meditate upon Sudhādedī; may Ardhanārīśvara inspire us. Thus one should recite ten times. Above that, one should recite the root mantra twenty-one times, and the nectar-seed syllable *vaṃ* twenty-one times. [Then] with the root mantra...
One should take the three fragrances.
One should draw the *yoni* in the center of the *sudhā*, and then two *hal* syllables within the *yoni*.
In the middle of that, one should meditate upon the Goddess Tāriṇī, the bestower of spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*).
To his left, the wise one should cause to be drawn a beautiful triangle joined with a bindu,
an outer circle, a hexagon, and another circle.
One should draw an auspicious eight-cornered [diagram] and worship it with the root mantra;
having placed the *śrīpātra* vessel there, one should bring the nectar (*sudhā*) into it.
Then, having taken a small amount of nectar from that vessel, one should bring some more;
and one should also offer what has been taken in another vessel, provided it is pure.
"Oṃ, may all the deities of travelers grant me auspiciousness! HAUṂ KṢAUṂ SVĀHĀ.

Having recited this, one should whirl it three times over a large vessel, then whirl it over the *śrīpātra*, and finally cast it at the root of a *vilva* tree, at a crossroads, into a river, a pond, or a courtesan’s house. Then, there—
Having invoked the Goddess, the Supreme Deity, according to the procedure prescribed in one's own ritual manual, and having worshipped her with the general and special arghya offerings and so forth,
one should then meditate upon the Goddess who delights in the bliss of nectar.
Always sixteen years of age, with a serene countenance and three eyes.
Abundantly radiant with red ornaments, adorned with various decorations,
she was intoxicated by Kāmadeva and assumed the form of a maiden.
The foremost of practitioners should meditate upon the Goddess who consists of Sadāśiva, whose heart is filled with the joy of passion, and who bestows great delight.

Then, having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) and performed the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) and other rites as prescribed in the respective *kalpas*, one should meditate there upon the mantra of the Supreme Deity—who generates manifold bliss—using saffron, camphor, fragrance, and sandalwood. One should cause the ritual substances to be offered. Then, with palms joined in reverence (*kṛtāñjali*):
Oṃ, salutations to that Goddess Sudhā, the bestower of the accomplishment of the stars;
to the Mother who grants merit, and to Maheśvarī for the sake of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having meditated especially upon the Great Goddess Kāmeśvarī,
she is the mother, the goddess Kāmeśvarī, and he is the father, Kāmeśvara.
Having meditated upon the union of the two, one should then worship the Supreme Deity;
he who worships either Kālikā or Tārakā is the best among men.
Indeed, this very purification occurs through the Mahācīna-krama alone;
for those fools who practice otherwise, everything becomes in vain.
Thus is the purification of the reality. Having brought meat there, one should purify it with the root mantra;
one should accomplish this while reciting this mantra with supreme devotion.
Oṃ. The wise, praising and ever-watchful, kindle that which is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Oṃ! The flesh of the boar, the great flesh, and the flesh of goats and so forth—all flesh except that of women—is for the sake of the purification of Tārā.
Flesh is the supreme cause that bestows ultimate bliss;
it is the substance dear to Tārā and is free from all defects.
Oṃ hauṃ kṣauṃ, purify, purify the flesh, the great flesh! Oṃ hauṃ kṣauṃ svāhā. Thus is the purification of the flesh.
Likewise, [one should contemplate] the golden form, the form of Viṣṇu, born from an egg.
To the god who is encircled by a great serpent, who has taken the form of a fish, and who is imperishable.
The fish known as Mahāmaha, who is always beloved by Tārā:
Oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ mauṃ vlaṃ saḥ saḥ saḥ, purify this fish!
"Śodhaya svāhā!"— thus is the purification of the fish.
Then, having formed the *yonimudrā* and gazed upon the *yonimudrā*,
recite this mantra, O child, for the sake of accomplishing all rites.
The supreme Yonividya, the Great Vidyā, known as Kāmākhyā, the bestower of desires,
the goddess who grants the attainment of all wishes, beginning with the seed-syllable of Kāma.
Oṃ klīṃ! O Kāmeśvarī! O Mahāmāyā! Klīṃ! Salutation to Kālikā.
Oṃ, [I praise] the Yoni-vidyā, the Great Vidyā, which bestows the fourfold aims of human existence.
In the opinion of Tārānātha, there is knowledge of the arts and crafts in the *Tara-taru*.

Oṃ kṣauṃ vluṃ hrauṃ hraḥ! O Yoni-Vidyā, O Yoni-Siddhā, O You who bring about the cause of the Yoni! You are to be known as the bestower of desires and the non-bestower of desires, the Great-Most-Great within the midst of the Tattvas.
Oṃ sauṃ bāle bāle Tripurasundarī, O you whose form is the Yoni! Grant me all success, grant it; perform the Yonimudrā, perform it, svāhā! Thus is the purification of the mudrās.
Then follows the purification of the Śakti: Oṃ aiṃ klīṃ Tripuradevī, O you who possess all powers!

Having recited "Śivatvaṃ dehi dehi Oṃ Auṃ" ten times over her head, and having performed the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* upon her body, one should perform the *ṛṣyādi-nyāsa* and the *karāṅga-nyāsa*. One should then recite the root mantra (*mūla*) one hundred times at her heart. This is the consecration of the Śakti (*śakti-saṃskāra*).
Having uttered the root mantra, the wise one should draw a triangle on his left;
there, in the center, he should write the syllable of modesty (hrīṃ), which is the very nature of the principle of desire.
There, worship should be performed even with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata); and having prostrated again and again before the practitioners and their wives, one should continue.
Having first offered water with a sense of modesty and having received permission from the practitioner,
and saying "I shall perform the libation," one performs the libation without withdrawing [the breath].
One should also employ the joining of the thumb with the ring finger of the left hand.

With "ha sa kṣa ma la va ra yūṃ ānandabhairavīṃ tarpayāmi svāhā," one should perform the triple libation at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) using pure *āsava*. In this same manner, [one should offer to] the Guru, the Paramaguru,
the Parāparaguru, and the Parameṣṭhiguru with "ha sa kṣa ma la va ra yūṃ."
"Ānandabhairavaṃ svāhā"—thus three times. Then, in the heart, having uttered the root mantra in that same form:
"I satiate the goddess Tārā, who is Bhīmā, Ekajaṭā, and the bestower of the supreme state—svāhā.
This applies everywhere regarding the Goddess. And so it is said in the *Tārānigama*:
When one performs the libation for Tārā, one should likewise perform the libation for the supreme Kālikā;
one should also perform the libation for the goddess Ṣoḍaśī, for otherwise the ritual act is fruitless.
That which is declared as the supreme Kālī is celebrated as Tārā;
she alone is the goddess Śrīṣoḍaśī, the Great Tripurasundarī.
He who meditates upon non-duality is indeed the venerable Sadāśiva;
he who meditates otherwise, O Maheśvara, is a fool.
He who takes refuge at the pair of feet [of the Lord] in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld shall become a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) conducive to great liberation.
Where there is enjoyment, there is no liberation;
where there is liberation, there is no enjoyment. [But this is not so] for those who are intent upon the gratification of Śrī Sundarī.
Both worldly enjoyment and liberation are indeed within the palm of one's hand.

Then, having drawn a triangle on the palm of one’s own right hand and having placed all things endowed with purity within the middle of that triangle, one should recite the *lajjābīja* ten times: *oṃ hrīṃ hrauṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ*.

AḤ! I purify the seed-principle (bījatattva) by means of the supreme principle (paramatattva) situated at the lower corner, svāhā! Having thus taken the portion for purification in the left hand, one should grasp it. Having taken the left-hand portion, [one recites]: OṂ HRĪṂ HAUṂ HRĀṂ HRĪṂ KAṂ KHAṂ GAṂ GHAṂ ṄAṂ CAṂ CHAṂ JAṂ JHAṂ...
ṆAṂ ṬAṂ ṬHAṂ ḌAṂ ḌHAṂ ṆAṂ TAṂ THAṂ; by means of the supreme reality abiding within the reality of the left,
I purify— svāhā!

Thus, as before. Then, having moved to the southern section: *oṃ hrīṃ hauṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ*, by means of the principle (*tattva*) situated in the southern corner, I purify the principle of power (*śaktitattva*); *svāhā*. Thus, as before. Then...

Having taken the middle portion, [recite]: *oṃ hrīṃ hrauṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ laṃ kṣaṃ māyātattvena māyātattvaṃ śodhayāmi svāhā*. Thus, as before. Then, one should give the vessel and the purification to the practitioners and the Śaktis; all according to the prescribed rule.
They perform the ritual action. Then, the vessel should be taken at the mouth of the Kuṇḍalinī.
The best of practitioners should recite the mantra seven times over the vessel;
having remembered the Guru, he should drink the liquor, which grants the fulfillment of all desires and aims.

Then, one should offer oblations into the mouth of Kuṇḍalinī preceded by the mantra. Having taken the first vessel and having taken the remains of the Śakti into the second vessel, one should drink. And so it is said:
"One should drink the wine that is the remains of the Śakti, and chew the food that is the remains of the Vīra."
Drinking separately from the remnants of a hero is proclaimed as the drinking of the animal (paśupāna).
For there is the hearing of censure regarding practitioners, and within the family [tradition], there is ignorance concerning violence;
or else, there is the censure of the Śakti-kaulas and the failure to worship the practitioners.
If one engages in sexual union with a Śakti out of lack of desire, or even through force,
or if one engages with a Śakti out of lust, there is no meditation nor any connection with the deity.
That worship of the lineage which is devoid of recitation and fire-offerings, lacking in devotion,
and performed openly before practitioners, results in a practitioner who remains dissatisfied.
Thus, a Kaula who is endowed with these qualities is proclaimed as one who has not fallen from the path.
Having placed the fifth [tattva] before him, he should perform the recitation (japa) in the fourth.
Drinking without recitation and worship is proclaimed as the drinking of a beast (paśu-pāna).
Now, the mantras for binding the bowl:

[This place] is drenched by the nectar of the moon shining from the crest of the illustrious Bhairava, and is worshipped by the hosts of Siddhas and by the multitudes of people who are yogis presiding over the sacred field (kṣetra).
I salute this great-souled ocean of bliss, the manifest nectar of the three sections, the first auspicious vessel held in the lotus-hand that bestows purity.

Golden, endowed with the dark digit (nīlakalā), possessing the yoga of great majesty, the Great Meat (mahāmāṃsaka), somewhat restless in its gaze, bestowing the excellent splendor of the sun, eternal— this knowledge, flowing forth from the great ocean of bliss and the like, grants supreme liberation.
Now I worship the second vessel, which is capable of awakening one's own self.
I pay homage to the third vessel, which holds a large lotus in the hand and a lotus at the base, beheld with the intellect and accompanied by the "burnt fish" [mudrā].
With supreme devotion, I worship the Yonimudrā, who has the form of a mudrā, who bestows accomplishments, and whose very nature is accomplishment; I bring the fourth [vow] to completion.
The linga is pervaded by the yoni; this is proclaimed as the fifth.
With that very nectar which has become [the essence], I fashion the fifth here.
I bow to the sixth worthy recipient (pātra), the gift bestowed at the feet of the Guru, which bestows eternal bliss and grants great joy.
Born from the seven oceans, auspicious and born from the waters of the ocean,
I take up the seventh nectar when the ocean has reached its shore.
The eightfold Durgā is the embodiment of power, the destroyer of the demon Mahiṣāsura;
she, the sustainer of the world, purifies [all], while in the ninth [form] she is the beloved of Śaṅkara.
The ten great vidyās are proclaimed as bestowers of the great siddhis;
and the Mohinī [is present] in the tenth hand for the destruction of great delusion.
I bow to those eleven Mahārudras, the bestowers of the wealth of supernatural powers (vasusiddhi),
who grant the sixty-four siddhis upon my eleventh hand.
In the twelfth [digit], the twelve Ādityas are ever intent upon offering libations;
I salute the twelfth in the form of the left eye.
In the thirteenth [chapter], the Great Vidyā Sāradā is fully extolled;
I bow to the Goddess who bestows the perfection of speech in the thirteenth vessel.
Thus concludes the salutation to the thirteen vessels, which always bestows happiness. As for whatever other variety of vessel-salutation is seen in another treatise, that—
This concerns the objects of Kālī, Tārā, Sundarī, Tripurā, and Itarā.
As long as the eye does not waver and the mind does not waver,
so long should the drinking be performed, which bestows the accomplishment of the mantra.
Having drunk again and again, having drunk again and again, he falls upon the ground;
rising up and drinking once more, rebirth is no longer found.

Now, regarding the exclusive Śrītārā as taught in the Tārānigama, here is the mantra for saluting all worthy recipients (*pātra*) in one place: Oṃ. I am not the doer, nor the one who causes action; I have no object of action.
I am not the enjoyer, nor the one who causes enjoyment, nor is there anything to be enjoyed. I am the conscious self (*cidātman*).

I am Viṣṇu myself, the very radiance, the teacher, and identical in form [to Him]. One should not remember nor worship another, having abandoned the first; there is no other austerity nor goal, having abandoned the first. Thus, one who is endowed with purity should drink [the nectar] everywhere. First, one should drink according to one's capacity. Then—

The Sequence of the Five Principles (Pañcatattvakrama). First, having taken the substance with the left hand using the drinking-mudrā in the form of a triangle, and having performed purification with the right hand, one recites the root mantra:
"This liquor conjoined with purification, salutation to the illustrious goddess Tārā Ekajaṭā Mahādevī. [This applies] everywhere.

For the purification and consecration, there is the recitation of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). Holding meat in the left hand and reciting the root mantra seven times—this is the purification of the meat. Homage to the venerable goddess Tārā Ekajaṭā. Then, taking fish in the left hand—this is the purification of the fish. Homage to the venerable Tārā.

"Salutation to the goddess Ekajaṭā. Then, having displayed the Śakti-liṅga mudrā, one should offer [the oblation] with the words: "This is the Śakti, the venerable Tārā, the goddess Ekajaṭā; for the sake of the conception of great bliss, protect, protect! Behold, behold! Be gracious, be gracious! Grant, grant me success in her womb! Oṃ oṃ oṃ svāhā. Thus it is offered.
Having bestowed bliss as is appropriate, having led the *śakti* from the other location to the *cakra*, having established her before oneself facing forward, having deposited the *bindu* upon her,
and having displayed the *yoniliṅgamudrā*, if she is uninitiated, one should whisper the seed-syllable of modesty (*lajjābīja*) into her ear.
With palms joined in reverence:
O Śaktirūpā! O Mahādevī! O You whose very nature is the perfection of the Yoni!
Be gracious, O creator of the worlds! O you whose form is Brahman!
The Great Vidyā is the form of the womb, bestowing the accomplishment of the womb;
from her emanation is born, and she is protected even as a son.
It dissolves again into the womb, which is the abode of creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
I shall accomplish the great mantra—by that, grant me success!
Having recited "Oṃ hauṃ hrauṃ klīṃ Kāmeśvari Mahātripure Tripurālaye!
Dehi dehi mamaiva siddhiṃ svāhā," and having chanted the mantra of liberation over the *liṅga* seven times,
becoming naked oneself and making her naked, one should behold the lotus and the reflection therein.
One should recite the mantra one hundred times at the navel while focusing on the solar orb, the fly-whisk, the fish, and likewise the peak.
Having recited it one hundred times within the center of the *yoni*, the wise practitioner should effect entry and meditate upon Goddess Pārvatī, who consists of the Great *Yoni*.
Having contemplated oneself as being of the very nature of Śiva, as the immutable Self in the form of Śiva, one should personally dispel all obstacles and become truly prosperous.
If a practitioner meditates [on this] while being full of desire, he is born as a lustful one;
he is cooked in a terrible hell, and there is no liberation for ten million births.
Therefore, with every effort, one should remain personally free from modification;
otherwise, there will be a loss of accomplishment, and one will fall into hell oneself.
Oṃ! In the fire whose nature is the consciousness of the navel, with the ladle of the mind and the oblation of knowledge, I perpetually offer the activity of the senses as a burnt offering.

"Oṃ, with the mind as the sacrificial ladle, I constantly offer my own self, blazing with the removal of merit and demerit, into the fire of the Self by means of the movement through the *suṣumṇā*, which is the activity of the senses. Thus one should renounce.
Then, remaining on that seat, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times. Thereafter, having washed the vessel—
Having written the seed-syllable of Māyā (*hrīṃ*) above the water, one should [use] clay situated there [with the mantra]:
*Oṃ yaṃ yaṃ spṛśāmi pādena yo māṃ paśyati cakṣuṣā*. (p. 56)
He himself becomes a slave if he should become equal to Śakra.

Having thus applied the forehead mark (*ṭīkā*), one should wander about. One should always place in the vessel a substance measuring one *tolaka* of silver. Having given it to the practitioners (*sādhakas*) and the empowered women (*śaktis*), one should bring back the vessel.
One should accomplish [the practice] through the three types of dispositions: the divine, the heroic, and the animal.
The Divyas, for the most part like gods, are devoted to virtuous conduct;
yet they particularly engage in the lending of money, teaching, and violence.
One should perform bathing, the twilight prayers, and worship—each three times—during the day. One should treat another's wife as one's own mother and others as one's own sons;
always recollecting the quality of sattva, one should certainly remain a celibate student.
Having beheld the face of a woman, or her breasts, or even her thighs, the best of practitioners should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and offer twelve pieces of gold.
One should satisfy with nectar the Goddess Tārā, the bestower of liberation;
even he would become Indra in person if he did not touch a woman.
Merely by touching a woman, one’s divine nature becomes futile;
as long as one must perform penance, one should avoid women.
Fish, meat, as well as oil, oily food, and sweetmeats—these should not be seen; likewise, women and Śūdras must not be looked upon, otherwise there will be a fall from one's state.

When his ascetic power has been perfected and he has fathered a son, he may approach his wife during her fertile period, avoiding the five forbidden lunar days; if he does so, he shall not fall from his spiritual state.

In this regard, the summary is as follows: the conduct of the heroes (*vīrācāra*) has been explained in brief in the *Bhāvasārāvalī*, and the conduct of the bound souls (*paśvācāra*) has been explained at the root of Kāmākhyā:
"One should not pursue a corpse, a woman, or even the earth."
One should not perform internal worship (antaryajana) in the case of the Kālī and Tārā Vidyās.
One should meditate upon the location of the sacred seat (pīṭha) and not show it to another's wife;
for the divine family of heroic beings is sublime, therefore the divine is praised.
Due to a lack of capacity, one may become a hero (*vīra*) but never a bound soul (*paśu*) in the Kali age;
by whatever means possible, one should avoid the state of being a bound soul.
What accomplishment is there in Bhārata by that [eating] which is done according to one's own whim?
Now follows a single verse from the *Tārānigama*, a hymn for peace:
Oṃ! Protect me, O you who are composed of compassion! Guard my beloved and true practitioner;
destroy, destroy my misfortunes! [Grant] unto me the lotus-face of my beloved.
O Śivā! O Bestower of Siddhis! Grant me eternally the perfection consisting of a mass of nectar upon nectar.
O Śivā! O Destroyer of bonds! Make [me] possess the knowledge that effects liberation.
Having recited the Śāntistotra, a person may dwell as he pleases;
however, that which exists in the center of the wheel must not be spoken of anywhere.
Even that conversation which takes place at dawn leads to destruction and to hell;
one should move about in the form of a wheel or even in the form of a line.
When the Bhairavī-cakra has entered, all castes become the best of the twice-born;
likewise, when the Bhairavī-cakra has ceased, they all become distinct once again.
Having bowed again and again to the one who had arrived from the discus to depart, [he thought]:
"Otherwise, his death would occur, and his destination would be the abode of Yama."
Whether traveling once toward another wheel situated at a distance or toward his own wheel,
he becomes a son of Tārakā and a lord of the eight supernatural powers (vasu-siddhi).
Upon seeing the Cakra, one obtains the fruit of thousands of horse-sacrifices, hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices, or even a hundred thousand tanks.
O Mahādeva! He who gives even a mere fraction [of wealth] to the Śaktis and to the Sādhaka obtains among the gods the fruit of ten million horse-sacrifices.
A Kaula should avoid these five: fasting, falling from a cliff, the twilight rituals, the observance of vows, and wandering to sacred pilgrimage sites.
One should always go to a great seat (mahāpīṭha); if not, then to an unsurpassed seat.
One must always go with effort to Tārāpura, which is a great seat.
O Goddess! By reciting [the mantra] three hundred thousand times, one becomes a master of all accomplishments.
To the east of Vaidyanātha, the Lord of the Wheel, lies this famous city of Tārāpura, rare on earth. One should go with effort to that place where the temple of Tārā-Śiva stands. This is the summary.

Thus ends the secret of the principles (*tattva*) and so forth in the third chapter of the *Tārārahasya*, composed by the venerable Brahmānanda, the wandering mendicant (*paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka*) and ascetic (*avadhūta*).
Now, the worship (*pūjā*). And likewise, in the *Tārānigama* and the *Tārāsāra*:
First, having purified the water and washed his hands and feet,
he should apply a *tilaka* with the root mantra and a *tripuṇḍra* mark with sacred ash.
Or else, [one may write] a commentary on red sandalwood or even on vermilion.

Oṃ maṇidhari! vajriṇi! sarvavaśaṅkari! huṃ phaṭ svāhā! Having tied the topknot with this [mantra], one performs the sipping of water (ācamana) with: Oṃ hrīṃ svāhā. The Guru, having first arrived at the door of the worship hall, consecrates the water with: Oṃ vajrodake huṃ phaṭ svāhā.

Oṃ, to the pure Dharma, pacify all three kinds of evil, having removed every conceptual construction, huṃ phaṭ svāhā! Having thus washed both hands and feet, taking ash for a *tilaka*, or a *tripuṇḍra* mark made from vermilion, *gorocanā*, or any other pigment, [one recites] the root mantra: Oṃ Maṇidhari!

Having tied the topknot with "O Vajriṇī! O Sarvavaśaṅkarī! Huṃ Phaṭ Svāhā," and having sipped water with "Oṃ Hrīṃ Svāhā," one should then contemplate the seat while remaining with palms joined in reverence.
Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one shall become a master of all accomplishments;
thereafter, having arranged Vairocana and the other deities, one should purify the ground.
Then, having purified the ground and purified a triangle beneath the seat,
one should subsequently purify the seat and destroy all obstacles.
Then follows the ritual application:
having visualized the moon there, one should imagine a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpadruma*) therein.
In the center of that is a jeweled pedestal, adorned with various kinds of gems.
Adorned with various ornaments and decorated by divine jewels,
it was filled on all sides with auspicious female spirits (śivās) rejoicing in flesh and bone.
In the four directions, one should visualize a funeral pyre composed of jackals, skulls, charcoal, and bones;
in its center, one should contemplate the Goddess according to the method of meditation as previously described.

Then, the rinsing of the mouth (ācamana): *oṃ ugratārāyai svāhā*, *oṃ ekajaṭāyai svāhā*, *oṃ nīlasarasvatyai svāhā*. Having thus rinsed the mouth, one should purify the hands with *oṃ hrīṃ svāhā* and cleanse the lips with the *kūrca* [mantra] using the *badhvīja*. Again, one should wash the hands with the *astra* [mantra].

At the mouth: *oṃ vairocanāya namaḥ*. At the nose: *oṃ śaṅkhapāṇḍarāya namaḥ*, *oṃ padmanābhāya namaḥ*. At the eyes: *oṃ asitāṅgāya namaḥ*, *oṃ māmakāya namaḥ*. At the ears: *oṃ māmakāya namaḥ*, *oṃ pāṇḍavāya namaḥ*, *oṃ*.

*Tārakāya namaḥ* (Salutation to Tāraka). At the heart: *Oṃ padmāntakāya namaḥ*. At the head: *Oṃ yamāntakāya namaḥ*. On the left arm: *Oṃ vighnāntakāya namaḥ*. On the right arm: *Oṃ narāntakāya namaḥ*. Thus is the sipping of water (*ācamana*) for Tārā. *Oṃ pavitre! bhūmi! huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Thus [is the purification].

Having consecrated the ground with the *yonimudrā* by reciting "Oṃ rakṣa rakṣa māṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā," one purifies the ground by sprinkling water. Then, having drawn a triangle beneath the seat and worshipped the seat by reciting "Oṃ āḥ surekhe! vajrarekhe! huṃ phaṭ svāhā," [one recites] "Oṃ hrīṃ."
"Obeisance to the one seated upon the lotus-throne of the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti-kamalāsana*). Having thus worshipped the seat, and having worshipped the seat again with "Oṃ,
drive away all obstacles, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," [one should know] that the seat is described in the *Tārārṇava*.
Whether it be a soft seat or likewise a tender head-ornament,
the falling of a fetus within the last eight months of pregnancy is called "mṛdu" (soft).
And the Cūḍākaraṇa ceremony is prescribed to take place within the interval of four years.
It was constructed from fifty kuśa leaves, purified with ashes and sand, and swept clean.
Furthermore, [a son] born from the womb of a Caṇḍālinī by the legitimate son of a Brāhmaṇa,
or born from the womb of a Brāhmaṇī by the legitimate son of a Caṇḍāla,
is called Kamalāsana; he bestows the attainment of mantras.

Having thus purified the lotus-seat (*kamalāsana*), one should dispel the obstacles by scattering flowers and unhusked rice with the mantra: *oṃ sarvavighnānutsāraya huṃ svāhā*. Then, having removed the celestial obstacles by gazing with the divine vision (*divyadṛṣṭi*) and the terrestrial obstacles by three strikes of the left foot—
Having prostrated before Gaṇeśa and the others, one should then perform the binding of the ten directions;
immediately thereafter, one should purify both hands with scents and flowers.

Having purified both hands with the syllable *phaṭ* using scents and flowers, one should perform the binding of the ten directions by clapping the hands three times and snapping the fingers. Having tied a knot in one's garment,
one should purify body, speech, and mind.
Having purified the flower, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Then, having propitiated the agent [of the rite], one should recite the root mantra ten times over the head.
The eleven [syllables] and the consecration mantra (pratiṣṭhāmantra) should be recited;
having performed the placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkānyāsa), one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) of the Mātṛkā.
One should place the limbs of the hands and the twelve sources (yonis) of the Mātṛkā.
Then one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) as well as the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the sages and so forth.
With the mantra: *oṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi mahāpratisare rakṣa rakṣa huṃ phaṭ svāhā*, one should purify body, speech, and mind. *Oṃ puṣpaketurājārhate śatāya samyak...* [etc.]
To the one who is bound: Oṃ puṣpe puṣpe mahāpuṣpe supuṣpe puṣpasambhave!

Having purified [the site] with "puṣpacayāvakīrṇe huṃ phaṭ svāhā," one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi). Placing both hands palm-upward upon one's own body, one should, with the mantra "haṃsaḥ," lead the Kuṇḍalinī, the individual soul (jīvātman),
and the twenty-four principles (tattvas) through the path of the Suṣumṇā into Śiva, the Supreme Self, who resides in the head.

Having joined [the syllables] and meditated on the red-colored syllable *hrīṃ* at the navel, one should burn the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) with the fire arising from it; then, having contemplated the yellow-colored syllable *strīṃ* at the heart, one should disperse the ashes with the wind arising from it; [and finally, one should contemplate] the white-colored syllable *huṃ*.
Having visualized [the syllable] at the head, one should bathe those bones with the nectar produced therefrom; then,
within that water which pervades the universe, from the syllable ĀḤ arises a red lotus, and upon it, from the syllable ṬĪ.
Upon that [lotus] is a white lotus; upon that, a syllable *hūṃ* resembling [the color] blue; and upon that, one should meditate on the Mother (*mātṛkā*) adorned with the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*.
Oṃ! She stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, she is formidable, and she is adorned with a garland of severed heads.
In the union of the sword and the knife, she holds them in her two right and left arms.
One should meditate on her who possesses a pair of hands joined with a skull and a blue lotus, whose single matted lock is tawny and fierce, and who is adorned by Akṣobhya upon her crown.
Akṣobhya is the three-fold form (Trimūrti) residing on the head of Hara, assuming the form of a serpent.
She whose eyes are the moon, sun, and fire, who is intoxicated by the great drink.

Having meditated thus, one should place a flower upon one's own head and, having worshipped by means of mental offerings according to the method of internal worship (*antaryajana*), one should prostrate. Then, having recited "Oṃ Āṃ Hrīṃ Kroṃ Svāhā" eleven times over one's own head and established [the deity there], one should stand with palms joined in reverence.
Her face, arms, waist, and chest are adorned with the fifty letters of the alphabet; she wears a radiant crown bound with a crescent moon and possesses full, lofty breasts.
With her lotus-like hands, she holds a mudrā, a rosary, a jar brimming with nectar, and the goddess of learning (Vidyā).
I take refuge in the Goddess of Speech, who bears the three eyes and possesses a brilliant white luster.
Having thus meditated upon the Mātṛkā, one should perform the Mātṛkā-nyāsa: *aṃ* namaḥ on the forehead; *āṃ* namaḥ on the mouth;
*iṃ* namaḥ on the right eye; *īṃ* namaḥ on the left eye; *uṃ* namaḥ on the right ear; *ūṃ* namaḥ on the left ear; *ṛṃ* namaḥ on the right nostril; *ṝṃ* namaḥ on the [left nostril].
*Vāma* (the left) is in the mind. *Ḷaṃ*, salutation to the right cheek; *ḹṃ*, salutation to the left cheek; *eṃ*, salutation to the upper lip;

*aiṃ*, salutation to the lower lip; *oṃ*, salutation to the upper teeth; *auṃ*, salutation to the lower teeth; *aṃ*, salutation to the *brahmarandhra*; *aḥ*, salutation to the mouth; *kaṃ*, salutation to the root of the right arm; *khaṃ*, salutation...

At the elbow: *gaṃ* namaḥ to the armor (*kavaca*). At the base of the fingers: *ghaṃ* namaḥ. At the tips of the fingers: *ṅaṃ* namaḥ. Likewise, with the right hand, [place] *caṃ*, *chaṃ*, *jaṃ*, *jhaṃ*, and *ñaṃ* on the root of the left upper arm, the four joints, and the tip [of the fingers].
Ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ at the four joints and the tips of the right foot; taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ at the four joints and the tips of the left foot; paṃ namo.

*Phaṃ* *namaḥ* on the right side; *vaṃ* *namaḥ* on the left side; *bhaṃ* *namaḥ* on the back; *maṃ* *namaḥ* at the navel; *yaṃ* *namaḥ* in the belly; *raṃ* *namaḥ* in the heart; *laṃ* *namaḥ* on the right shoulder;
*vaṃ* *namaḥ* on the crown of the head; *śaṃ* *namaḥ* on the left shoulder; *ṣaṃ* *namaḥ* from the heart to the right hand.

*Namo* from the heart and so forth on the left hand; *saṃ namo* from the heart and so forth on the right foot; *haṃ namo* from the heart and so forth on the left foot; *laṃ namo* from the heart and so forth on the abdomen; *kṣaṃ namo* from the heart and so forth on the mouth.
[One should place them] on the forehead, the perimeter of the face, the two eyes, the two ears, and the two nostrils.
Either on the cheeks, the lips, or especially on the rows of teeth.
The wise one should again place the letters beginning with *a* at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) and in the mouth.
The wise one should place the combination of the index finger and the middle finger upon the letter *a*.
Then, by joining the middle and ring fingers, one should place [the mudrā] in the mouth;
likewise, by joining the middle finger and the thumb, one should place it on the two eyes;
and by joining the ring finger and the thumb, it is to be placed on the two ears.
One should place [the mudrā] upon the nose by joining the index finger and the thumb;
one should always place it upon the cheeks by joining the ring finger and the middle finger.
The placement [of mantras] should also be performed on the two lips using the joint of the thumb;
taking the tip of the middle finger, it should be placed upon the teeth.
The best of practitioners, having assumed the Vidyāmudrā with both hands, should place the tip of the thumb at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) and the palms at the mouth.
One should place [the syllables] on the hands, feet, sides, back, and at the navel;
in the rite of the Mātṛkā-nyāsa, the palm is said to have the form of the heart.
Or again, on the hump of the shoulders, or everywhere on the hands.

Then, with the root mantra, one should perform the three pervasive placements (vyāpaka): from the head down to the feet, from the feet up to the head, and from the head down to the heart; and from the heart up to the mouth. One should then assign the limbs and the fingers using the groups of consonants beginning with 'a' and so forth.
Aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ, homage to the heart. Iṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ īṃ, svāhā to the head. Uṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ.

Ūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock (śikhā). Eṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ aiṃ, huṃ to the hair (kaca). Oṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ auṃ, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes (netratraya). Aṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ aḥ, [phaṭ] to the weapon (astra) with the palms and backs of the hands.

Phaṭ! Aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ, salutation to the two thumbs (aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ). Iṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ īṃ, svāhā to the two index fingers (tarjanībhyāṃ svāhā). Uṃ ṭa ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ Ūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the two middle fingers (madhyamābhyāṃ vaṣaṭ). Eṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ...
Aiṃ, to the two ring fingers, Huṃ. Oṃ Paṃ Phaṃ Baṃ Bhaṃ Maṃ Auṃ, to the two little fingers, Vauṣaṭ. Aṃ Yaṃ Raṃ Laṃ Vaṃ Śaṃ Ṣaṃ Saṃ Haṃ Laṃ Kṣaṃ Aḥ, to the palms and backs of the hands, Astrāya Phaṭ.
The most excellent practitioner should also place the twelvefold sciences upon the head,
the mouth, the throat, the heart, and likewise upon the belly.
And in the lotus that is the support of non-existence, [she resides] everywhere— in the feet, the arms, the womb, the altar,
as the eternal Yoni, and likewise in the form of the Yoni.
She who is in the center of the womb, perfected by the womb, fashioned by the womb, and the giver of the womb;
she who takes away the womb, to be accomplished through the womb, possessing knowledge of the womb, and the protector of the womb.
Likewise, the placement of others is for the sake of the accomplishment of the fourfold aims, beginning with the source of merit.

With the deer-gesture (*mṛgamudrā*), [one should worship]: *oṃ yonivedyāyai namaḥ* on the head; *oṃ yoninityāyai namaḥ* on the face; *oṃ yonirūpāyai namaḥ* on the throat; *oṃ yonimadhyāyai namaḥ* on the heart;
*oṃ yonisiddhāyai namaḥ* on the abdomen; *oṃ yonikḷptāyai namaḥ* on the navel.

At the *mūlādhāra*: Oṃ, salutation to Yonidā. At the right foot: Oṃ, salutation to Yonihā. At the left foot: Oṃ, salutation to Yonisādhyā. At the right arm: Oṃ, salutation to Yonijñānā. At the left arm: Oṃ, salutation to Yonipā. At all limbs: Oṃ, salutation to Yonipuṇyā. Thus.
One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*). Thus ends the twelve-yoni placement (*dvādaśayoninyāsa*).
Holding the right nostril with the thumb of the right hand and having recited the root mantra sixteen times, one should fill the breath. Then, holding both nostrils—
Having performed the retention of breath after reciting [the mantra] sixty-four times, one should hold [the nostrils] with the little and ring fingers at the left nostril.
One should exhale through the right [nostril] by reciting [the mantra] thirty-two times; then, having filled [it] again through the right, one should exhale through the left.
The holding of the nostrils is performed with the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb.
That should be known as prāṇāyāma, consisting of inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka).
One should perform this in the same manner three times; this is *prāṇāyāma*. At the head:
*oṃ akṣobhyarṣaye namaḥ*. In the mouth: *oṃ vṛhaspaticchandase namaḥ*. In the heart: *śrīmattārāyai ekajaṭāyai devyai namaḥ*. At the *mūlādhāra*: *huṃ* to the seed-syllable.
*Namaḥ* at the feet; *phaṭ*, *namaḥ* to Śakti; *namaḥ* to the *kīlaka* of one’s own seed-syllable (*bīja*) on all limbs. Thus is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and the others.
Having then performed the placement of the throne (*pīṭha-nyāsa*), one should thereafter place the powers of the throne (*pīṭha-śakti*).
Having performed that placement (nyāsa), one should then perform the placement of the seed-syllables (bīja).
Having performed the placement of the Karāṅgas and the Ṣaḍaṅgas, one should then place the seed-syllables (varṇas).
After purifying the yantra within the body, one should perform the worship of the seat (pīṭhapūjā).
Having first performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā) for Gaṇeśa, Vaṭuka, Kṣetrapāla, and the Yoginīs, one should then worship the Śaktis of the pedestal.
Then, having divided [the vessel] into six parts and having prepared the *arghya* offering again, the mantra-practitioner,
having performed the fivefold pervasive [protection], should worship the Supreme Deity.
Placing the hand upon the heart with the *mṛgamudrā*, [one should offer salutation] to the filaments of the heart-lotus:
*Oṃ śmaśānāya namaḥ* (Oṃ, salutation to the cremation ground); *Oṃ kalpavṛkṣāya namaḥ* (Oṃ, salutation to the wish-fulfilling tree); *Oṃ maṇipīṭhāya namaḥ* (Oṃ, salutation to the jewel-throne);
*Oṃ nānālaṅkārebhyo namaḥ* (Oṃ, salutation to the various ornaments); *Oṃ munibhyo namaḥ* (Oṃ, salutation to the sages); *Oṃ devebhyo namaḥ* (Oṃ, salutation to the gods). *Oṃ*.
Homage to the jackals rejoicing in flesh, marrow, and bones! In the four directions:
Oṃ, homage to the corpse, the skull, the funeral pyre, the embers, and the bones! Thus is the *pīṭha-nyāsa*.
In the heart: Oṃ, homage to Lakṣmī; Oṃ, homage to Sarasvatī; Oṃ, homage to Prīti; Oṃ...
Salutation to Kīrti; Oṃ, salutation to Śānti; salutation to Tuṣṭi; Oṃ, salutation to Puṣṭi—thus is the ritual placement of the pedestal powers (pīṭhaśaktinyāsa).

"Oṃ, svāhā to the principle of the Self (ātmatattva)"—thus from the base up to the heart. "Oṃ, svāhā to the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva)"—thus from the heart up to the mouth. "Oṃ, svāhā to the principle of Śiva (śivatattva)"—thus from the mouth up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). This is the ritual placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa).

Having divided the mantra into five sections, one should place the first seed-syllable ending with *namaḥ* from the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) to the forehead. One should place the second seed-syllable ending with *namaḥ* from the forehead to the mouth.
One should place the third seed-syllable ending with *namaḥ* from the mouth to the throat. [One should place the fourth seed-syllable ending with *namaḥ*] from the throat to the heart.
The fourth syllable is *namaḥ*. From the heart to the mouth, the fifth syllable is *namaḥ*. This is the seed-syllable placement (*bījanyāsa*).
The letter *ha* joined with the letter *ra*, endowed with the six long vowels.
Having fashioned it with a crescent moon, the supreme practitioner should install it.
Ekajaṭā and Tāriṇī are to be deposited, and likewise Vajrodakā;
thereafter Ugrajaṭā is to be deposited, and likewise Mahāpratisarā.
Then, on the hands and limbs, one should perform the six-limbed ritual starting with Piṅgograikajaṭā.
Likewise: *hrāṃ ekajaṭāyai aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*; *hrīṃ tāriṇyai tarjanībhyāṃ svāhā*; *hrūṃ vajrodake madhyamābhyāṃ vaṣaṭ*;
*hraim ugrajaṭe anāmikābhyāṃ huṃ*; *hrauṃ mahāpratisare*.
*Vauṣaṭ* with the two little fingers. *Hraḥ piṅgograikajaṭe karatalapṛṣṭhābhyām astrāya phaṭ*. Thus is the ritual assignment (*nyāsa*) of the hands and limbs.
*Hrāṃ ekajaṭāyai hṛdayāya namaḥ*. *Hrīṃ tāriṇyai śirase svāhā*.

Hrūṃ vajrodake, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock (śikhā). Hraiṃ ugrajaṭe, huṃ to the armor (kavaca). Hrauṃ mahāpratisare, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes (netratraya). Hraḥ piṅgograikajaṭe, phaṭ to the weapon (astra) with both palms and backs of the hands. Thus is the ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa).

Aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ; *namas* to the heart. Eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ; *namas* to the right arm. Ṅaṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ; *namas* to the left arm. Ṇaṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ...

*Dhaṃ naṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ namo* to the right foot. *Maṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ namo* to the left foot. Then, having extracted the Yantra of the glorious Ekajaṭā, one should consecrate it with: *Oṃ āḥ surekhe*.
"Vajrarekhe hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ. Having thus displayed the *yoni-mudrā*, one should purify the *yantra*. Then, one should begin the worship: starting from the east, "Oṃ hrīṃ gāṃ to Gaṇapati, namaḥ."
In the south: *Oṃ hrīṃ vāṃ vaṭukāya namaḥ*. In the west: *Oṃ hrīṃ kṣeṃ kṣetrapālāya namaḥ*. In the north: *Oṃ hrīṃ yāṃ yoginībhyo namaḥ*.

Having performed the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭhapūjā*) according to the procedure for the placement on the pedestal (*pīṭhanyāsa*), [one should worship] the pedestal-energies (*pīṭhaśakti*) on the eight petals starting from the east.

Having worshipped [the seat] in the center with "Hasauḥ, obeisance to Sadāśiva, the Great Preta, the Lotus Throne," then, having fashioned a maṇḍala consisting of a dot, a triangle, a circle, and a square in one's own left, [one says] there: "Obeisance to the place for the *arghya* of the venerable goddess Ekajaṭā. Having invoked the tripod (*tripadikā*) there,
Having sprinkled it with water and washed the vessel with "Phaṭ," having placed it there,

[one says] "Oṃ, salutation to the Arghya-vessel of the goddess Śrīmad-Ekajaṭā. Then, having filled it with the root mantra and having cast red sandalwood, bilva leaves, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, and so forth;

Having filled the conch with water consisting of the nectar born from the *bindu* using the letters of the *mātṛkā* in reverse order along with the root mantra, one should invoke the *arghya* there with the "O Gaṅgā" verse and the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*; then, having rendered it nectar with the syllable *vaṃ* and the *dhenu-mudrā*, one should display the *yoni-mudrā* and the *matsya-mudrā*.
Having covered [the vessel] there, meditated upon the Goddess, offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), and performed the assignment of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga-vinyāsa*),

one should recite the root mantra ten times there. Then, having sprinkled oneself and the ritual implements with those waters and flowers, and having prepared the fivefold water offering (*pañcārghya*), one performs the fivefold pervasive [assignment].
Having performed [the ritual], one should meditate upon the Goddess.
One should meditate upon the venerable Goddess Tārakā with the tortoise hand-gesture (*kacchapa-mudrā*);
and one who especially desires the fruit [of practice] should meditate upon her with the womb-gesture (*yoni-mudrā*).
The Supreme Goddess stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture with her foot placed upon the heart of a corpse, uttering a terrible *aṭṭahāsa* laugh;
she holds a sword, a crescent moon, a *kartri*, and a skull-cup in her arms, and is born from the seed-syllable *Huṃ*.
Dwarfed in form, with a vast blue mass of matted hair adorned with a single serpent, the fierce Tārā herself destroys the dullness of the three worlds by casting it into her skull-bowl.
Having meditated thus, having placed that flower upon the yantra, and having contemplated the secret of meditation, one should invoke her as follows:
"She who is entirely blue like a fresh rain-cloud, the pot-bellied one..."
Her waist is beautified by being draped in a tiger skin;
she has full, elevated breasts and three round, red eyes, with an extremely dark mass of matted hair upon her back.
Her head is exquisitely adorned with the hoods of nāgas fashioned by the great deity Akṣobhya; on both sides hang garlands of blue lotuses,
and she possesses five skulls in the form of a white triangle representing the five mudrās.
She has a mass of matted hair that is intensely blue, with long, flowing tresses like those of a yak;
she wears a bracelet made of the white-colored Takṣaka nāga,
a short necklace made of red-colored nāgas, and a long necklace made of the multicolored Śeṣa nāga.

She has a golden complexion and wears small snake-rings on her toes; she has a snake-girdle made of slightly reddish snakes and bracelets made of snakes as dark as dūrvā grass leaves; her three eyes are formed by the moon, the sun, and fire, and her right eye possesses the luster of ten million rising suns.
She has one hundred million crescent moons as her left eye and one hundred thousand suns as her right eye;

she has a trembling tongue; her right leg is drawn up and placed upon the heart of Mahākāla in the form of a corpse, while her left leg is extended and placed upon the two feet of the corpse—by this, she stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture.
She is beautiful with garlands of severed heads whose hair is entangled with one another as fresh blood flows from their recently cut necks;

she is adorned with all the ornaments of women, she deludes through great infatuation yet bestows great liberation; she is incapable of inverted sexual union, her face smiling with the intensity of passion.
In her lower right hand she holds a *kartri*,

and above that she holds a *khaḍga* sword with a laugh-like blade (*candrahāsa*) marked by a hundred *lakṣa*s; in her upper left hand she holds a slightly blooming red *nāgakeśara* flower from which blue lotuses (*nīlotpala*) have dripped with nectar, for the purpose of removing fear from all disciples.

Having meditated upon her— born from the seed-syllable *huṃ*, adorned with a skull-bowl below and a freshly severed head upon her arm, the cutter and destroyer of all cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍas*), sixteen years of age, and the bestower of all knowledge— one should invoke her.
Oṃ! O Queen of the Gods! You who are easily accessible through devotion! You who are accompanied by your retinue!
As long as I worship you, remain steadfast here.
Having spoken thus, with palms joined upward: "O Śrīmad-Ekajaṭā! O Goddess! Come, come here!

With palms joined downward: "Stay, stay here! With the thumb and fist of the womb-gesture: "Be present, be present here! Then, with that downward-facing gesture, having rotated one's own hand which was held steady here—
Bestow your blessing here; accept my worship.
The letter Ā, conjoined with the Bindu and adorned with the Māyā-pāśa,
followed by Vahni-jāyā and ending with Haṃsa— this is declared to be the Pratiṣṭhā mantra.

Oṃ hrīṃ kroṃ svāhā. Haṃsaḥ! The vital breaths (prāṇas) of the glorious deity Ekajaṭā are here; likewise, the life-force (jīva) is established here; likewise, all the sense-faculties (indriyas) are established here.
Thus, speech, mind, eyes, ears, nose, and breath, having come here, may they remain happily for a long time.

*svāhā*. Thus, one should establish [the offering] with the tips of the ring finger and thumb joined together. Then, having recited the root mantra ten times and displayed the *dhenu*, *yoni*, *matsya*, *aṅkuśa*, *śaṅkha*, *khaḍga*, *mṛga*, and *gālinī* mudrās, one says: "O Goddess Śrīmadekajaṭā! Accept this vajra-flower! *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*."
Having thus offered handfuls of flowers (puṣpāñjali), one should perform the worship:
the seat, welcome, water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamanīyaka),
the honey-mixture (madhuparka), further sipping water, bathing, garments, and ornaments.

One should worship with fragrant flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and prostrations—either with the ten services (*daśopacāra*) or the five services (*pañcopacāra*). Thinking with the realization of the supreme person, "I am he," one should worship while reciting: *oṃ vajrapuṣpaṃ pratīccha huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This is [the procedure].

Having taken the water for the feet (*pādya*) with the words "Homage! Water for the feet!", one should offer it by opening the fist with the thumb and index finger extended over it, saying: "To the deity Ekajaṭā, this water for the feet; homage! Likewise, [one offers] this water of honor (*arghya*).
Svāhā!
One should offer water for the feet at the feet and present the respectful offering (arghya) upon the head;
likewise, one should offer fragrance on the forehead and flowers at the feet.

"This is for bathing, svadhā. With the *mṛgamudrā*, "this is fragrance, namaḥ. With the *añjali* mudrā, "flowers, vauṣaṭ. Then, having brought the bell to one's left, [worship] the bell with fragrance and flowers, reciting: "Oṃ jayadhvanimantramātaḥ svāhā."
Having worshipped [the incense], having placed it upon the vessel, and having recited the worship mantra,
holding it in the left hand, one offers it saying, "This is the incense, Svadhā. Then, performing the deer-mudrā (*mṛgamudrā*),
while ringing the bell with the left hand, one directs the fragrance of the incense toward the nostrils.
One should cause [the enemy] to be slain. Likewise: "This lamp, svāhā! Having offered the lamp up to the point of sight, one should perform the *nīrājana* ceremony.

Likewise, all other items such as garlands and so forth should be offered. Having drawn a triangle on one's left, one should bring the food offering (*naivedya*) there, transform it into nectar using the *dhenumudrā* while reciting "raṃ," display the *yonimudrā*, and then, having recited the root mantra ten times over it, protect it with the weapon mantra (*astra*) "phaṭ" and [display] the *gālinīmudrā*.
Having displayed it and held it with the ring finger and thumb of the left hand, one should offer water from the *arghya* vessel while saying:
"This food offering, together with its accessories, is for the venerable goddess Ekajaṭā; obeisance.
However, one who is not a woman or a Śūdra, having offered water with the mantra "Oṃ, you are the spreader of nectar, svāhā," [should hold it] in the left hand.

Having formed the *grāsa-mudrā* with the right hand, one should display the *mudrās* for the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth. Then, one should conclude the offering of water for drinking, followed by betel, the remains of the *culvaka*, and so on, accompanied by the ringing of the bell. Having thus worshipped with services according to one's capacity, one should perform the *yoni-mudrā*.

Having said, "O Goddess! Command me; I shall worship your retinue," and having worshipped the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), one should perform the worship everywhere, beginning with the goddess's crown, using the mantra: *oṃ akṣobhya vajrapuṣpaṃ pratīccha huṃ phaṭ svāhā*, and so forth. [One should likewise worship] the sword in the upper right hand of the goddess.

Having worshipped the flaying knife below that [hand], the blue lotus in the upper left hand, and below that, the skull-cup containing a freshly severed head, one should worship the lineage of gurus starting from the northwest and extending to the northeast (the Śiva-corner).
Having worshipped there alone Ūrdhvakeśa, Vyomakeśa, Nīlakaṇṭha, Vṛṣadhvaja, and ending with Ānandanātha, one shall obtain the fruit.
One should worship these— Tārāvatī, Bhānumatī, Jayā, Vidyā, Mahodarī, and Ambā— at the end [of the sequence], for the sake of attaining one's desired goals and liberation.
Vasiṣṭha, Mīnanātha, Harinātha, Kuleśvara, Virūpākṣa, Maheśvara, Sukha, and Pārijāta; Mahākāla, Rudrāṇī, Ugrā, Bhīmā, Ghorā, Bhrāmarī, Kālakartrī, and Viśvarūpā. Om.
*Ūrddhvakeśānandanātha*, accept this *vajrapuṣpa*, *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Likewise for *Vyomakeśānandanātha*, *Nīlakaṇṭhānandanātha*, and *Vṛṣadhvajānandanātha*.
And likewise for *Tārāvatyambā*, *Bhānumatyambā*, *Jayāvatyambā*, and *Vidyāvatyambā*.
[The lineage of] Mahodaryambā, as well as Avaśiṣṭhānandanātha,
Mīnanāthānandanātha, Harināthānandanātha, Kuleśvarānandanātha, Maheśvarānandanātha, Sukhānandanātha, and Pārijātānandanātha.
Likewise, [the goddesses] Mahākālarudrāṇyambā, Ugrāmbā, Bhīmāmbā, Ghorāmbā, Bhrāmaryambā, Kālarātryambā, and Viśvarūpāmbā. Then, starting from the east:
