One should worship on the eight petals in counter-clockwise order: "Oṃ Virocana, accept this vajra-flower! Huṃ Phaṭ Svāhā! Likewise, at the eastern gate: "O Śaṅkhapāṇḍara, Padmanābha, Asitāṅga, Pāṇḍara, Tāraka, Padmāntaka, accept this vajra-flower! Huṃ Phaṭ Svāhā! Thus [one worships].

Likewise, having worshipped Yamāntaka in the north, Vighnāntaka behind him (in the west), and Narāntaka in the south, and having offered five handfuls of flowers and honored the Goddess with water for the feet, the guest-offering, and so forth, one should draw a triangle, a hexagon, a circle, and a square on the left, and therein—

Having taken a common vessel filled with meat, rice, curd, turmeric, burnt fish, liquor, oil-cake, salt, and fresh ginger— considering these as not forbidden— and having taken water in the right hand, [recite]: *Oṃ hrīṃ,
O Goddess Śrīmad-Ekajaṭā, accept, accept, cause to be accepted this offering brought by me.*
"Grant me peace! Act! Act! Having repeatedly drawn forth the supreme vidyā, break! break! cut! cut! pierce! pierce! bring all the world under control! Oṃ hrauṃ svāhā!
Having recited this three times, one should offer the bali-oblation.
As it is stated in the *Kālikākalpa*: "The offering of one's own bodily blood—[this applies] to all that in the worship of Kālikā, but never in the context of Tārā."
If one's own bodily blood is offered to Tārā,
Tārā will always be angry with him, and he shall not obtain the fruit of worship.
A triangle, an octagon, a circle, and a square—
this arrangement of places is recommended for the offering of oblations during the worship of the Savior (Tāraka).
Having uttered "Oṃ Hrīṃ Ekajaṭā," and immediately thereafter "Devī," [one should then recite] the phrase "to the Great Lord of Yakṣas, that which is offered by me."
Having uttered the *vali* mantra, one should take hold of the pair; immediately thereafter, one should cause [the disciple] to hear it.
One should cause them to grasp the two feet and perform the rite for my peace (*śānti*).
Having repeatedly drawn forth the two *kuru*s and the *paravidyā*,
one should then utter the pair of *truṭi*s, and after that, the pair of *chindhi*s.
Having uttered the *bhindhi-yugma*, bring the entire world under control.
Having uttered the *lajjā-tāra*, one should offer the oblation (*bali*) and recite the triad.
Then, having again prepared the *arghya*, [one should address] "Oṃ hauṃ aiṃ, O Goddess Śrīmadekajaṭā, mine..."

Having recited, "O you who have mastered all sciences, *siddhya siddhya*, accept this *arghya*; grant the status of Lord of All Speech, *svāhā*," and having said "Victory! Victory!", one should offer the *nīrājana* lamp before placing [the offering] upon the head of the Goddess.
Having recited the mantra as much as possible and offered it, one should give water into the left hand of the Goddess.
Therefore, in all cases, the recitation of your armor-mantras and so forth must be preceded by the family rites (kulakriyā) and other preliminary practices.
Then, preceded by the sounding of bells and musical instruments, a person should perform circumambulation three times,
keeping the right hand raised.
From the southern direction one should go toward the northwestern direction, remaining there for a short while facing Śāṅkarī;
then, having returned to the south, one should prostrate while standing before her.
One should prostrate seven times and perform circumambulation three times;
then, falling prostrate like a staff upon the ground, who indeed would not obtain fruit?
Having joined the tips of the fingers together with a well-composed mind,
one should form a triangular shape and slightly incline toward the left side.
Bowing with the chest, the head, the back, the two hands, and likewise the knees,
and by joining the nose and chin, one shall attain perfection.
Now, the procedure for recitation:
One should recite the *kuluṅkā* mantra ten times on the head for the sake of mantra-perfection;
the *setu* mantra seven times on the mouth; and the *puṭa* mantra with the *praṇava* on the heart.
The best of practitioners, devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma), should first recite his own mantra; then [the syllables] *kulvukā*,
followed by the second [syllable] enriched with the moon (*candra*), as well as *lajjā* and the goad (*aṅkuśa*).

One should recite "Āṃ Hrīṃ Krauṃ" ten times over the head; one should recite "Oṃ" seven times as a dam over the mouth; and one should recite the mantra encased by the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) seven times over the heart.

In all cases, first comes breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). Then the *setu*, then the *mahāsetu*, then the *mantraśikhā*—one should recite "oṃ hauṃ aiṃ" seven times. Then the *mantraprāṇa*—"kalarī"—seven times. Then one should recite [the main mantra] one thousand times, or one hundred and eight, or twenty. Then...
Taking a flower from the water in the palm of the hand, [one should say]: "Oṃ! You are the protector of the most secret of secrets; accept this recitation performed by us.
O Goddess, may success be mine through your grace, for you are present here."
Thus, one should offer the recitation into the left hand of the Goddess. Then follows the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma).

This is the procedure for recitation. Recitation performed for specific desires (kāmyajapa) shall be explained in the section on preparatory rites (puraścaraṇa). For daily recitation (nityajapa), this very [procedure] is the scriptural authority (nigama).
One should recite the mantra one thousand times for the sake of attaining success in dharma and liberation;
however, one hundred and eight recitations are for the attainment of the fruit of worship.

One should indeed recite the mantra twenty times for the sake of accomplishing the worship; this applies to the *Tārāsāra* regarding recitation other than the actual worship. As long as the supreme preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) has not been performed, [the practice is incomplete].
O Śiva, one should certainly not perform more than a thousand [recitations].
O child, the practitioner who, though possessed by agitation, recites with undistracted mind more than a thousand times, should offer it among thousands.

By this [rule], one who has not performed the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) should not recite [the mantra] more than a thousand times. If one should recite ten thousand times at once, then having recited a thousand times, one should offer it.
One should recite the mantra a thousand times during the rite of *puraścaraṇa*.
He should recite it exactly one hundred times; never more than that.
Then, taking the arghya water, [one should say]: "Oṃ!

Whatever [was done] by me previously, through the authority of my life-force, intellect, body, and dharma, in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, by means of mind, speech, action, the two hands, the feet, the stomach, and the genitals—whatever was remembered..."
As it has been said: "Whatever has been done, may all that become an offering to Brahman; may my entire [work] be perfectly offered to the deity Śrīmad-Ekajaṭā.

Then, having dismissed [the deity] with the words "Forgive me" using the *saṃhāramudrā*, one should offer obeisance to Oṃ Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālinī in the northeast within a triangle. Then, having accepted a portion of the food offering (*naivedya*)— such as the foot-salve, sandalwood paste used for smearing the yantra, and so forth— with that [remnant], and having given the rest to the [other] Śaktis:
"One should dwell as one pleases"— thus concludes the ritual procedure for the worship of Ekajaṭā.
[One should meditate upon] the Goddess Mahāmāyā, standing in the pratyālīḍha posture, possessing three eyes, enriched with all ornaments, and having the supreme luster of a great sapphire.
The best of practitioners should visualize the deity holding a sword and a noose in his right hands, and an utpala lotus and a wine-cup above his left hands, together with the Goddess.
Having meditated thus, one should worship her upon the yantra described in that *kalpa*. This concludes the worship of Tārā.
Now follows the worship of Kāmatārā. Upon the yantra described in that *kalpa*:
[one should worship] the Great Goddess Ghorahāsya, the Savior (Tāriṇī), whose form is the syllable *tāra*.
A water-pot, a blue lotus, and likewise a most excellent sword.
Clad in a tiger skin and adorned with all ornaments,
she wears a serpent necklace upon her breast and possesses the form of the Great Yoga.

Having meditated thus and invoked [the deity] as before, one performs everything [else]. This is the worship of Kāmatārā. Regarding the various throne-energies (pīṭhaśakti) such as Lakṣmī and others mentioned in the manual for Ugratārā, they are not present here; rather:
One should worship Icchā, Jñānā, and Kriyā, as well as Kāminī who grants desires, Rati who is dear to Rati, and Ratidā.
Upon the corpse is Mahādevī, joined with the laughter of the Lord of Corpses;
she is Ugratārā, the supreme among the supreme, intent upon inverted sexual union.
The supreme Tāriṇī is depicted holding a curved knife and a sword in her right hands;
in her left portion, a blue lotus is held, and beneath that, a wine-cup is traditionally described.
She is beautiful with a garland of severed heads, adorned with streams of blood,
possessing a terrifying laugh and three eyes, and she is the constant bestower of wisdom.
She has a single braid and a great braid, adorned with the king of serpents;
she is endowed with golden crowns and graced with white teeth.
Having meditated thus, as before. This concludes the worship of Ugratārā.
For those who are the consort of Śambhu and the beloved of Mahākāla, the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) is joined with the mantra of twenty-four syllables; this much is the distinction.
I always salute Nīlavāṇī, who has the luster of a mass of blue collyrium,
who is adorned with the ornaments of women, and whose waist is draped in a tiger skin.
The Goddess is entwined by a serpent, wearing a necklace of hooded snakes;
her right foot is extended by way of the serpent’s head,
while her left foot rests upon a corpse at the navel, her heart filled with the joy of amorous play.
She is of the nature of darkness, vast, deluding the universe, and a terrible woman of desire;
she is the bee at the mouth of Śiva, auspicious, and standing in the pratyālīḍha posture.
Her hair was perpetually flowing, adorned with the processed tail-hair of a yak;
and upon her head she bore [the mark] endowed with various jewels, which destroys great sins.
For the sake of attaining all accomplishments, one should visualize Sarasvatī, who has a blue complexion, holds a skull and a sword, possesses a blue voice, and wears a garland of wood-apples.
Having meditated thus, everything is as before. One should worship the lotus, sword, staff, noose, skull-cup, trident, mace, lotus, wheel, and so forth, in the eight directions of the yantra;
this is the distinction. This concludes the worship of Nīlasāradā and Mahānīlasarasvatī. Then—

The daily fire-oblation (nityahoma) should be performed according to one's capacity. Thus it is said in the Nigama: "Indeed, by him who offers even a single oblation to Tārakā, the sin committed throughout ten million lifetimes is destroyed in that very instant."
Then follows the offering of the sacrificial victim (bali):
either a goat, or a buffalo, or a pig, or a bird,
or an elephant, or even a mouse, or a cat, or a ram.
Having offered [this] to the Great Goddess, he shall become a leader of the *kula*.
Having brought the sacrificial offering (*bali*) before him and having displayed the *yonimudrā*, [he should proceed].
Holding her throat with the right hand, one should place it upon the left shoulder:
"O Śrīmad-Ekajaṭā, O Goddess, O Supreme among Devas, accept this offering!
Grant me the accomplishment of mantras and grant me the accomplishment of the creeper (latāsiddhi)!"

Oṃ hrīṃ hāṃ huṃ aiṃ aiṃ, O bestower of all accomplishments! Grant, grant me the accomplishment of the four aims; accept, accept the offering, svāhā! Having thus presented [the offering] and worshipped the sword with water, flowers, and so forth, one should strike it once and cut [the victim]. This is the offering of the bali.
Having offered the liquor and the food, one should experience bliss;
then the worship should be performed, for otherwise it would be fruitless.
Having divided consciousness into four parts, [one should offer] with the first [part] by means of the *tattvamudrā*: "Oṃ! O Consciousness! Born of Brahman! Daughter of Brahman! Ever sinless!
For the sake of the satisfaction of the Bhairavas, be forever pure!"
Oṃ, obeisance to Brāhmī, svāhā! Thus one should cast [the offering] upon the ground.
Oṃ, O Goddess who brings about the root of accomplishment! O awakener of those with inferior understanding!
O subduer of kings and subjects! O wielder of the trident at the throats of enemies!
Aiṃ, obeisance to Kṣatriyā.
Oṃ, I bow, I bow to you, O revealer of the path of Yoga!
O Mother, conqueror of the three worlds, grant me the fruit of samādhi.
Hrīṃ, obeisance to Vaiśyā.
Oṃ! O you who blaze with the fuel of ignorance, O flame of fire whose nature is Brahman!
Grant me the oblation of bliss, joy, and perfect knowledge.
*Klīṃ śūdrāyai namaḥ svāhā*. Then, having drawn a triangle in the center of that, [one should recite]: *Oṃ amṛte! amṛtodbhave! amṛtavarṣiṇi! priye! amṛtam ākarṣaya ākarṣaya svāhā*.
Then, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) as before with the *Tattvamudrā*. Then, having cast a little [of the water] upon the ground...
"Oṃ aiṃ aiṃ, speak, speak, O Goddess of Speech! Be established upon my tongue;
destroy all enemies, destroy them, svāhā!"—with this, one should perform the oblation.
There Kamalā sits, intent with palms joined in reverence; there Sāradā holds her lute;
and there Tārā recollects the words of her beloved, as does Umā, for the sake of his command.
In the auspicious *Tārārahasya*, composed by Brahmānanda as a manual for excellent practice,
this third chapter— which bestows the accomplishment of all goals— concerns the rules for conduct and other observances.
Now begins the fourth chapter. Now, the sixfold [method]:
the *praṇava* enclosed by the letters of the *mātṛkā* in the place of the *mātṛkā*.
"O Pārvatī, one should place the phoneme enclosed by that very [syllable] right there. Thus it is said in the *Yāmala*.
Having made the *mātṛkā* alone, then the *mātṛkā* enclosed by the *tāra*, then that same [mātṛkā] enclosed by the *tāra*, and finally the *lajjā* enclosed by the *mātṛkā*.
Enveloped by *lajjā*, that [mantra] should be placed by the best of practitioners;
likewise, the woman is enveloped by the *mātṛkā*, and the *mātṛkā* by the woman.
The *kūrca* is enclosed by the *mātṛkā*, and the letters are enclosed by the *kūrca*;
likewise, the *mātṛkā* is enclosed by the *asta*, and the *asta* is similarly enclosed by the *mātṛkā*.
The mantra is enclosed by the *mātṛkā*, and that [mātṛkā] is enclosed by the mantra.
He who performs ten thousand [breaths] through the practice of the Vāyu-kumbhaka becomes a great yogi and beholds the Goddess with his own eyes.
If a mantra is deficient in six ways, it becomes weak;
it will not bestow accomplishment, nor will it ever grant liberation.
Aṃ tāraṃ aṃ oṃ aṃ namaḥ | Oṃ aṃ oṃ namaḥ | Strīṃ aṃ strīṃ aṃ namaḥ | Strīṃ aṃ strīṃ namaḥ | Aṃ hrīṃ aṃ namaḥ | Hrīṃ aṃ hrīṃ namaḥ | Aṃ chaṃ aṃ namaḥ | Hūṃ aṃ hūṃ namaḥ | Aṃ phaṭ aṃ namaḥ |
*phaṭ aṃ phaṭ namaḥ* | *aṃ mūlaṃ aṃ namaḥ* | *mūlaṃ aṃ mūlaṃ namaḥ* | *aṃ namaḥ aṃ lajjā aṃ namaḥ lajjā aṃ lajjā namaḥ* (p. 77).

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) by means of the wind-retention (*vāyudhāraṇa*), reciting: *aṃ badhūm aṃ namaḥ; aṃ kūrcam aṃ namaḥ kūrcam aṃ kūrcam namaḥ; aṃ phaṭ aṃ namaḥ phaṭ aṃ phaṭ namaḥ; aṃ mūlam aṃ namaḥ mūlam aṃ mūlam namaḥ*, [one should proceed] with the root mantra (*mūla*).
One should perform the sevenfold pervasion. Thus is the Guhya-ṣoḍhā.
Hrīṃ Aiṃ Hauṃ Klīṃ Huṃ Phaṭ. [The mantras are] Lañjā, the Vāgbhava-bīja, Prāsāda, and Kāma.
Then, having likewise assigned the armor-seed-syllable and the weapon-mantra, one shall attain success.
Thus is the Mahāṣoḍhā.
One should recite the mantra "dhūṃ dhūṃ dhūmāvati! svāhā" ten times.
In the sequence of the deposition of the letters (varṇanyāsa), the Vadhū is encapsulated by Māyā.
Having joined the syllables in pairs, the best of practitioners should perform the placement;
having then performed the sixfold placement, he shall attain great accomplishment.

Having performed the "folded" (*puṭita*) arrangement as before, one should perform the sixfold deposition (*ṣaḍdhā nyāsa*) in fifty locations, just like the deposition of the phonemes (*varṇanyāsa*). This is the Great Sixfold (*Mahāṣoḍhā*).
O Child! That by which the Sixfold is performed daily is the most magnificent.
He shall attain the accomplishment of mantras, for he indeed hears a voice in his dreams.
Thus ends the third section on the Sixfold [Rite] (*ṣoḍhā*) in the fourth chapter of the *Tārā-rahasya*, composed by the wandering mendicant (*paramahaṃsaparivrājaka*) Avadhūta Brahmānanda.
The sixfold [rite] at night consists of fish, meat, and so forth, combined with the finest rice and other offerings.
Then, having performed the evening twilight ritual (saṃdhyā), one should practice yoga;
the base of the support, the root, and the tip of the neck are proclaimed as the spinal column (merudaṇḍa).
Residing there, one dwells in the world with three crores of sacred fords within the body;
on its left side, in that portion, is the channel called Iḍā, which bestows the accomplishment of all goals.
To the right is the auspicious Piṅgalā channel, which embodies all sacred fords;
in front of Meru is the Suṣumnā, the meritorious channel that bestows everything.
In the center of that is Citriṇī, and in the center of that, Vajrā is said to be;
she is known as the Brahma-nāḍī, which bestows the bliss of Brahman.
Like a blue lotus and its stalk, it shines in the very center;
through the union with the steady wind, the moving and the unmoving indeed remain established.
That Kuṇḍalinī-śakti is proclaimed as the breath (nāsāvāyu);
indeed, through the union with Māyā, eight [powers] are established therein.
The silver shines and remains in the form of a tilaka;
likewise, the channels, devoid of consciousness, remain bound within the body.
It abides there, relying upon that holy ford, the sacred great seat (mahāpīṭha);
and the yantra and the deity are firmly established there at the root,
just as the lotus at the base of Mount Meru is proclaimed to be the root-support (mūlādhāra).
It is four finger-breadths wide and four finger-breadths high;
it has four petals, red petals, and is triangular, with a pericarp at its center.
In the midst of that, indeed, is the form of the Bindu, conjoined with the power (śakti) of Kākinī;
it is called the Svayambhū-liṅga, golden-hued and most beautiful.
Having encircled the five barley-measures of the beautiful Great Liṅga, the supreme Kuṇḍalinī Śakti should sport.
Having the form of a restless serpent, she assumes the nature of Brahman;
she always consists of great yoga, appearing as three and a half coils.
Even when being recited by the six-footed [bee], it should never touch the *liṅga*;
it resembles ten million suns and is as cool as ten million moons.
The Lord of Gods, whose form is like the flickering flash of lightning and whose nature is that of the Supreme Brahman,
sports upon the eastern petal in his Virāṭ form.
Joined with the power of the digit of consciousness (citkalā), Mahākāla is praised with palms joined in reverence;
and on the right, he is joined with the power of Kālikā.
Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Mahālakṣmī lineage, remains in the west with supreme devotion toward her whose nature is great wisdom.
The supreme Kuṇḍalinī is praised with supreme devotion and feeling;
and in the north, Mahādeva Śaṅkara is present together with Pārvatī.
When one ever hears even a single word from the speech of those who praise the goddess Tāriṇī, the great sovereign lady in the form of a serpent.
"O Mahādeva! Only they would indeed be capable of performing creation, maintenance, and even dissolution; well said, well said, you have explained it."
When the *liṅga* is smeared, then the man should go to sleep;
that supreme power (*paramā śakti*) will always remain steady when [the breath] is fixed in a stable position.
At that time, the world will undoubtedly become a field of merit,
when she bestows supreme bliss upon the head of the Liṅga.
The living being becomes capable of recitation (japa), and therein the sound bestows perfection;
when the one whose form is Brahman places her tail upon the top of the linga.
One who violates the teacher’s bed, approaches the wife of a Brahmin, or has intercourse with a young girl— [for these sins],
there should be a six-petalled lotus at the base of the linga, red and pale-white in color.
In the center of that is a pale-red liṅga, the essence of the origin of the universe,
conjoined with the power Hākinī, which bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as Rudra, Bhaga, Candra,
and Śacīpati shine in the midst of the petals, endowed with all powers.
The supreme *liṅga*, which bestows the accomplishment of all desires and goals, is praised;
one should diligently cause the *kuṇḍalinī* to move from the *mūlādhāra* to that [place].
O Maheśvarī! by the mere touch of that [lotus], its northern petal, which is its upper face, shall not move upon the lotus even for one possessed of great power.
But all those residing there go to heaven along with their families;
having gathered together, they all praise her who bestows spiritual perfection.
At the navel is an eight-petalled lotus with the luster of a fresh cloud;
there is the Viśvāntaka-liṅga, conjoined with the power of Śākinī.
Indra, Vahni, Pitṛpati, Nairṛta, Varuṇa, Marut, Kuvera, and Īśāna are there, each endowed with his own respective Śakti.
There, having placed [the deity] within the center of the lotus, supported by the Brahma-nāḍī, one should then visualize its vessels and the northern [vessel].
Those respective gods, having gone there, praise him endowed with devotion;
and then one should meditate upon a sixteen-petaled lotus within the heart.
The great white [lotus], the great red lotus, and the petal shaped like an elephant's forehead;
Indra, Candra, Guru, Śukra, Vāmadeva, and the Lord of Śivā.
Īśvara, Śaṅkara, Kṛṣṇa, Vāmadeva, Kuleśvara,
Kamalānāyaka, Kopa, Kāmarūpa, and Kṛpāmaya.
And in the sixteen Karaṇas, accompanied by his respective consorts,
he always praises the Great Liṅga Maheśvara with devotion.
One should meditate upon the Supreme-Beyond-the-Supreme, conjoined with the power of the Ḍākinī;
having ascended that path, one should bring the Goddess there.
To its left shines the individual soul (jīva), and below it is indeed sin;
the heart is joined with the drinking of liquor, and the two hips with violating the teacher’s bed.
Endowed with adamantine teeth and adorned with delicate teeth,
possessing a great body, he is always present in the heart, free from the great gods.
A mark on the nails taken by gold is considered the worst, being possessed of all defects;
it is ninefold in nature, devoid of liberation, and bereft of the traditional conduct of the lineage.
One should meditate upon it as bestowing desires through its desire-granting form, and likewise as providing delight and [the realization of] defects;
thereafter, one should contemplate a most beautiful ten-petalled lotus.
The great lotus of blue color bestows all accomplishments;
the great liṅga named Kāma shines together with the beloved woman.
Kāmadeva, Śāmba, Kāmācāra, Kāmuka,
the leader of passionate women, Kāma, Brahmananda, and Kuleśvara.
The Lord of the Three Worlds, the eternally blissful Kaula, abiding in the ten-petaled lotus,
together with his respective Śaktis, praises the supreme Kuṇḍalī.
On the forehead is the eye-leaf, endowed with the Brahma-liṅga;
Viṣṇu together with Śakti and Rudra together with Tārā offer praise.
Having pierced through that, the goddess, the supreme Kuṇḍalinī Śakti,
has gone from the channel at the tip of the spinal column (merudaṇḍa) to the thousand-spoked [lotus] which faces downward.
Consequently, the gods residing in the three worlds are present right there with their powers;
it is a twelve-petalled lotus endowed with the three channels (nāḍīs).
There, the pericarp of the triangle is endowed with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
the couch is possessed of teeth and eyes, and is joined with the Śakti and the Vajra.
There too, the venerable Guru himself, devoted to the welfare of all beings,
[beheld] the Lord, white as camphor, the imperishable embodiment of Brahman.
One should meditate upon the supreme Śiva, whose face is turned toward the north;
all the deities, beginning with the Root [deity], praise Him, the Cause of All.
One should contemplate the great power Kuṇḍalinī, who is like a lotus, at the forehead.
One should meditate upon her in the form of Śiva while leading her to the left side;
having established Rati on the left, this is for the sake of the Guru’s own perfect accomplishment.
Having arisen there as well, O Goddess, the Guru beheld Maheśvarī in her embodied form, consisting of mantra, yet she was devoid of power by the Guru.
By means of that, one stands above, destroying great delusion;
from her left big toe, the supreme nectar is said to flow.
Having drunk that, the individual soul (jīva) lives perpetually through both pleasure and pain;
if, by means of the yoga of cultivating meditative absorption (bhāvanā), one causes it to enter the channel (nāḍī),
one attains the great siddhi and certainly becomes immortal.
Thus ends the Essence of Yoga regarding the Tārā-yoga. (p.
82) Therein dwells Kamalā with palms joined in reverence, and Sāradā holding a lute.

Recalling Tārā, who is to be worshipped, and the words of Umā as the cause, this fourth chapter— which bestows the accomplishment of all aims— is concluded within the auspicious *Tārārahasya*, the method for excellent practice composed by Brahmānanda, concerning the rules of Yogācāra.
Thus ends the Tārārahasyatantra.
